a-knock-in-the-night.title: A Knock in the Night
a-knock-in-the-night.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: Someone is knocking on your door in the dark: small fists, over and over. When you open it, [who:regard-neighbour]'s eldest is standing there in her nightdress. "Mam can't breathe," she says. "Da says come."

Next door, the house is hot and full of smoke from a fire built too high. [who:regard-neighbour] is in the bed by the hearth, propped up on every pillow in the house. The cough from the docks has gone down into her chest. Every breath is a fight, and she is losing it. Her husband stands at the foot of the bed with his hat in his hands, as if he is waiting to be told what to do.

You sit with her. Near the end she takes your wrist, and pulls you close so the children will not hear.

{if [q:trait] != 4}"Don't let them put me on the cart," she whispers. "Not the fires. Promise me. We're counted. We've always been counted." She looks past you at her children. "And the roll. When the convoy comes. Make sure they get what's theirs."{else}"I know you don't think much of us," she whispers. "Don't let them put me on the cart anyway. Not the fires. Not in front of the children." Her grip is stronger than it should be. "Please."{/if}

She dies a little before dawn, with the fire still roaring. Her husband sends the eldest running for the death-watch, as the law says he has to. Then the family sit down around the bed with the body, to keep it company until the priestess comes, and to watch it. In the city, everyone knows why you watch.

branches.title: Sit with her until the end
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stay, and sit with the family and the body until the priestess comes.

success.title: Before dawn
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You sit with them until it is light.

a-neighbour-dies.title: The Death-Watch
a-neighbour-dies.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The death-watch priestess comes up the street at first light, in grey, with a leather bag on a strap across her body: the nail-bag. She is younger than you expected, and she looks as if she has not slept. She has been up all night at other doors.

She stands at the foot of the bed and looks at the body for a long moment. She writes the death in a small book: the name, the house, the hour. Then she turns to the husband.

"For the Seal, with the prayers, the nail and the entry in the register, the church asks a month's wages," she says. "I'm sorry. That's the church's price, not mine."

The husband turns out his purse on the table. It is not a month's wages. It is not half of one. The children are watching.

"If you can't pay," the priestess says, gently, "she can't lie here. The law won't let her. The city's cart will come for her this morning, and she'll go to the fires outside the walls." She does not look at you. She does not have to. You are the only other person in the room with a purse.

branches.title: Pay for the Seal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Put your purse on the table beside the husband's, and tell the priestess to count out what the Seal costs.

success.title: The family owes you
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She counts it out carefully, coin by coin, and gives you back what is left, which is not much. "[who:regard-priestess]," she says, as if you had asked. "I'll remember who paid."

She seals the body with the whole family around the bed. She says every word of the prayers slowly and clearly, the way they are meant to be said, and she lets the children hold the candle. When it is done, the husband takes both your hands and cannot speak. "We'll pay you back," he says at last. "Every coin. I swear it." You both know how long that will take.

branches.title: Let the city burn the body
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Keep your purse in your pocket. It is not your money to spend, and it was not your family.

success.title: The city's cart
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The priestess waits a moment longer, then nods, as if she expected nothing else. "[who:regard-priestess]," she tells you, coldly, when you ask her name. "In case you need me for your own."

The cart comes at mid-morning. Two carters carry the body out in a sheet while the children scream. The husband stands in the doorway and watches it go down the street toward the gate, and then he turns and looks at you, and goes inside and shuts the door. The whole street saw.

branches.title: Bargain with the priestess
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take the priestess aside, and bargain with her: whatever the family has, for the Seal. Make her see it is that, or the cart.

success.title: What the family has, and more
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She listens to you with her arms folded. "You know it isn't enough," she says. "I know it," you say. For a moment you think she will walk out.

Then she sighs, and takes the husband's coins, and seals the body with the prayers said properly. Afterwards, when she thinks nobody is looking, she takes coins out of her own purse and puts them in the church's box with the rest. "[who:regard-priestess]," she says when she sees you watching. "And you didn't see that."

success.title: The ford ahead

against-the-wall.title: Against the Wall
against-the-wall.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The watch comes through the half-counted district at dawn, looking for deaths nobody reported and bodies somebody hid. Everyone has to stand with their backs to the city wall while they search. A watchman goes down the line with a lamp, holding it up to each face while a clerk writes.

Beside you is the family who put up the next lean-to last week: a mother and father, three thin children, and a grandmother so old she has to be held up, praying under her breath. They do not know yet how this works. Then something happens.

branches.title: Devout
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: When the lamp reaches you, hold up the saint's medal you wear at your neck, and pray aloud with the grandmother.

success.title: A medal in the lamplight
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The watchman holds the lamp on your medal, then on your face. "Very holy," he says. "Half-counted, and holy." The clerk writes it down.

When the watch has moved on, the grandmother takes your hand in both of hers. "You know the old prayers," she says. "Nobody knows them any more." The mother tells you the family's name, [who:regard-family], and asks if you would teach the children that prayer. "In case," she says, and doesn't say in case of what.

branches.title: Doubter
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The watchman asks you if anyone has died in your lean-to. Tell him the church would take its price for a body either way, dead or alive.

success.title: The church's price
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He looks at you for a long moment over the lamp. "Half-counted," he says to the clerk, "and a mouth on it. Write that." The clerk writes that.

The father of the family beside you laughs under his breath, and turns it into a cough when the watchman looks round. When the watch has moved on, he tells you their name: "[who:regard-family]. Where we come from, people who say things like that don't last. I like it here already."

branches.title: Soft-hearted
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The family's youngest child has wandered out of the line into the watch's path. Step out, pull the child back, and hold them behind you.

success.title: Behind you
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: A watchman's boot swings where the child was standing a moment ago. He turns on you instead. "Did I say move?" The clerk writes you down as half-counted, and adds a note that you moved.

The mother takes the child back from you with shaking hands. "[who:regard-family]," she says, when the watch has gone. "That's our name. I won't forget what you did." The grandmother just looks at you and nods, slowly, as if she has seen it all before.

branches.title: Hard-hearted
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The sergeant asks the line who is new in the row. Point at the family beside you.

success.title: The new ones
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The watch turns the family's lean-to inside out while they stand and watch. They throw the bedding in the mud and break the only pot. They find nothing. The clerk writes you down too, as half-counted. "Useful," the sergeant says to him. "Remember the face." Now the watch knows you are someone who talks.

When they have gone, the father tells you their name, very flatly, so that you will know he knows yours: "[who:regard-family]." The grandmother spits on the ground between you.

branches.title: Proud
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The sergeant orders everyone down on their knees against the wall. Stay on your feet.

success.title: On your feet
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You stay standing while the whole line kneels. It takes the watchman a moment to notice. Then he puts his cudgel into the back of your knees, and you go down hard in the mud. "Half-counted," he tells the clerk, "and stiff-necked. Put a mark by it."

When they have gone, the father of the family beside you helps you up. "[who:regard-family]," he says. "Brave, or stupid. Where we come from, it's the same word."

branches.title: Grasping
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask the watchman, loud enough for the clerk to hear, what the watch pays for a name: a death somebody didn't report.

success.title: What a name is worth
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He tells you, without lowering his voice. It is more than you thought, and less than a life is worth. The clerk writes you down: half-counted, and willing. "Come to the gate if you hear of anything," the sergeant says. "Ask for me."

The family beside you heard every word. When the watch has gone, the mother tells you their name, [who:regard-family], carefully, like someone handing over something that might be used against them.

branches.title: Curious
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask the watchman whose death they are really looking for this time.

success.title: Whose death
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: "Nobody's in particular," he says. "Any death that isn't on the count. Any body that hasn't been sealed or burned." He leans closer with the lamp. "Why? Do you know of one?" The clerk writes you down as half-counted, and the watchman makes a note for asking.

When they have moved on, the family beside you tell you their name, [who:regard-family], in whispers. "Do they come often?" the mother asks. "Often enough," you say.

branches.title: Loyal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Two watchmen drag the old man who taught you to set snares out of the line. Walk beside him to the end of the row, so he is not alone.

success.title: To the end of the row
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: They let you. At the end of the row the sergeant looks at the old man's face and says, "Not him," and they let him go. They wanted someone else. The clerk writes you down as half-counted, and notes whom you walked with.

When you get back to your place against the wall, the family beside you have been watching. "[who:regard-family]," the father says. "That's our name. That's the kind of neighbour I hoped we'd get."

branches.title: Hot-tempered
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A watchman kicks down the pole that holds up your lean-to, for no reason at all. Shove him away from it.

success.title: The pole
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He stumbles back into the mud, and three watchmen have their cudgels up at once. The sergeant pulls them off before it goes further. "Half-counted," he tells the clerk, "and a mark by the name. A big one." The clerk makes a big one.

When they have gone, the father of the family helps you put your pole back up. "[who:regard-family]," he says. "I'd have done the same, once. Before I had children."

branches.title: Teetotal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The father of the family passes a jug along the wall to steady everyone's nerves while they wait. Pass it on without drinking.

success.title: Without the jug
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He takes it back and drinks your share himself. "More for me," he says. "[who:regard-family]. That's us. You'll want to keep a clear head round here, I suppose."

The watchman reaches you, lifts the lamp to your face, and moves on. The clerk writes you down as half-counted with everyone else against the wall. For once, nobody has noticed you at all.

branches.title: Hearty appetite
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The watch sometimes takes food when they search. Eat your bread against the wall, all of it, before they can get to it.

success.title: Nothing left to take
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The family's three children watch every mouthful you take. None of them says anything. The youngest licks her lips.

The watchman reaches you as you swallow the last of it. "Half-counted," he tells the clerk, "and well fed, apparently." When they have gone, the mother tells you the family's name: "[who:regard-family]." She does not ask for anything. She does not have to.

branches.title: Grave-shy
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Down the row, the watch drags a body out from under a lean-to, wrapped in a blanket. Turn your face to the wall until it is gone.

success.title: Face to the wall
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You press your forehead against the cold stone and breathe. Behind you there is shouting, and a woman crying, and the sound of something being dragged. A watchman writes down everyone who looks away. You are in his book now: half-counted, and noted.

When you turn round, the grandmother of the family is watching you. "They frighten you," she says. "Good. They should." The mother tells you the family's name: "[who:regard-family]."

an-uncounted-death.title: An Uncounted Death
an-uncounted-death.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: Everyone in the district knows the rules. A death has to be reported to the watch at the gate. A priest has to see the body. If the dead person was on the count and the family can pay, the body is sealed. If not, the city's cart takes it to the night fires, and it burns as a sentence, with the whole district watching.

The grandmother was on no count. The family cannot pay. So the cart will come for her either way, unless the family burn her first, themselves, their own way. That is heresy and a crime, and the watch will be round within the hour.

There is one other way. The death-watch priestess comes out to the gate most mornings. She cannot stop the sentence, but she could seal the body before the cart takes it, so it would at least go to the fire whole and prayed over. The family do not want her. The family may not get a choice.

branches.title: Help them burn her themselves
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Help the family drag wood out to the ditch behind the lean-tos, and burn her there, now, before the watch comes.

success.title: The old way
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The wood is wet and the fire is slow to take. The father says words over it in a language you don't know, and the mother holds the children's faces so they watch. When it catches, it catches hard. She will not rise now, and she will not go on the city's cart.

Then you see the smoke going up, straight and grey in the still morning air, where the whole wall can see it. Up on the walk along the top of the wall, a watchman stops and looks down. Then he turns and runs toward the gate.

branches.title: Fetch the priestess
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Run to the gate and find the death-watch priestess, and bring her back before the watch gets here.

success.title: Sealed before the sentence
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She is at the gate with her bag, already tired at dawn. She comes without arguing. "[who:regard-priestess]," she says as she walks, when you ask. "Is the family counted? No. Then I'm sorry. I can't stop the cart."

But she kneels in the lean-to and seals the old woman herself, with the prayers said properly, before the cart comes. "She'll go to the fire whole, and prayed over," she tells the family. "That's what I can give her." The mother will not look at her, or at you. They wanted their own fire, and you brought them the church.

branches.title: Report it
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Walk to the gate and report the death to the watch, before somebody else does and names you with the family.

success.title: The watch takes the body
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The sergeant at the gate writes it down and thanks you for your honesty, and makes a small mark beside your name that you suspect is a good one. "Helpful," he says. "We like helpful."

The watch get to the lean-to before the family's fire is lit. They take the grandmother on the cart, and the mother screams at them, and at you. The whole row sees who walked up behind the watch, and who walked away.

below-deck.title: Below Deck
below-deck.intro: PLACEHOLDER: The hold of your barge, where the passengers sleep on the grain sacks with their packs for pillows. It smells of wet wool and tar, and the river knocks against the planks all night. There is a lamp by the ladder, and a bucket nobody wants to be near.{if [q:hunger] >= 3} Your stomach has been complaining since morning.{/if}{if [q:cold] >= 3} Down here the cold comes up through the sacks, and you cannot stop shivering.{/if}

branches.title: Eat from your provisions
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Sit on your sacks and eat from the rations in your pack.

success.title: A meal
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Hard bread, a piece of cheese going sweaty in its cloth, and river water from the barrel by the ladder. It is not much, but it fills the hole, and for a while you stop thinking about food.

charter-day.title: Charter Day
charter-day.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: Charter day, in your street. The convoy is due any day with the new king's charter, and the council has ordered a feast to welcome it. Your neighbours are carrying benches out and hanging green branches over the doors.

A clerk of the count comes down the street with a pot of paint and a watchman to carry his book. At every door he paints how many in the house are counted.

The woman who took the house next to yours at midsummer is setting up a table beside yours, with two small children who keep running off. You have nodded to each other every morning since, and never talked. Then something happens.

branches.title: Devout
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The parish priest comes to bless the feast bread at the top of the street. Kneel on the cobbles for the blessing, in your good clothes.

success.title: The bread blessed
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You kneel until the priest has gone past, and your knees are wet through. When you stand up, the woman from next door is kneeling beside you with a child under each arm, trying to keep them still.

"I never know if it counts when they won't shut their eyes," she says, and laughs. "[who:regard-neighbour]. We should have done this months ago." Behind you the clerk paints your door: your household, all counted.

branches.title: Doubter
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: While the clerk paints your door, tell the woman from next door that the paint washes off in the first good rain, and so does the count.

success.title: Paint and rain
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She glances at the clerk, who does not turn round, then bites her lip to keep from laughing. "Don't," she says. "He'll paint us out." She holds out her hand. "[who:regard-neighbour]. My husband says the same thing, but only indoors."

The clerk finishes your door without a word: all counted. He paints the number a little harder than he needs to.

branches.title: Soft-hearted
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A beggar from the half-counted district is waiting at the end of the street, where the watch will move him on soon. Fill a plate from your table and carry it to him.

success.title: A plate for the beggar
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He eats it standing up, fast, with his back to the wall, before the watch can see. When you turn round, the woman from next door is behind you with a second plate.

"I saw you," she says. "I didn't want to be the only one who didn't." She gives the beggar the plate. "[who:regard-neighbour]. My mother was half-counted, before she married." Back at your house, the clerk has painted your door: all counted.

branches.title: Hard-hearted
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The woman from next door has no bench for the feast, and asks to borrow yours. Say no.

success.title: Your bench
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She goes red, and says of course, it's no matter. Her family end up sitting on their doorstep for the feast, the children on the cold stone.

Later she tells you her name anyway, stiffly: "[who:regard-neighbour]. So you know whose bench it was you kept." The clerk paints your door while she is still standing there: all counted.

branches.title: Proud
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The clerk paints the count on your door crooked, with a drip. Tell him your family has been counted since the walls went up, and make him paint it again.

success.title: Painted twice
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He looks at you, and at the door, and at the watchman, who shrugs. Then he paints it again, slowly and straight: all counted.

The woman from next door watched the whole thing with her hand over her mouth. He painted her door crooked too. "Would you make him do mine?" she asks. "[who:regard-neighbour]. I'd never dare."

branches.title: Grasping
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The woman from next door has no wine for the toast to the charter. Offer to sell her a jug of yours, at twice what you paid for it.

success.title: Half now, half later
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She hesitates, then counts out half the money. "The rest when the charter comes," she says. "My husband's promised a better place at the mills, once it's read." She tells you her name so you know who owes you: "[who:regard-neighbour]."

The clerk paints your door while you are counting the coins: all counted.

branches.title: Curious
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask the clerk what the new mark is that he is painting beside the number on some doors.

success.title: The new mark
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He does not stop painting. "It's for the new roll," he says. "The charter comes with a new roll of citizens. Some houses have people on it who aren't counted yet, and will be." He paints your door: all counted, and no new mark.

The woman from next door was listening. "Ours has the mark," she says quietly, as if it might be taken away. "My husband's brother. [who:regard-neighbour], by the way. I'm next door."

branches.title: Loyal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The clerk has no name in his book for the house next door, and is about to walk past it. Tell him the woman there has lived in it since midsummer, and you see her every day.

success.title: On your word
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The clerk asks you her name, and you realise you don't know it. She tells him herself: "[who:regard-neighbour]." He writes her into his book on your word, and paints both your doors: all counted.

"Nobody's ever spoken for me before," she says afterwards. "Not in this city."

branches.title: Hot-tempered
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A guildsman from the top of the street shoves the woman's table aside to put his own in the best place. Shove it back.

success.title: The best place
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: His table goes over and his bread goes in the gutter. He opens his mouth, looks at your face, and closes it again, and carries his table somewhere else, swearing.

The woman from next door helps you set her table straight. "My husband would have let him," she says. "[who:regard-neighbour]. Remind me to stay on your good side." The clerk paints your door as if nothing happened: all counted.

branches.title: Teetotal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The street's cask is opened for the first toast to the charter. Raise a cup of water instead of wine.

success.title: Water for the charter
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: A few people look at your cup. The woman from next door sees the water, raises her own cup to you anyway, and clinks it against yours.

"To the charter," she says, "and to clear heads." She drinks. "[who:regard-neighbour]. My father drank. I understand." The clerk paints your door: all counted.

branches.title: Hearty appetite
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take a meat pie from the feast table before the bread has been blessed, while nobody is looking.

success.title: Before the blessing
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: Somebody is looking: the woman from next door, who catches you with your mouth full. She laughs so hard her children come running to see why.

"I won't tell," she says, and takes a pie herself. "[who:regard-neighbour]. Now we're both damned." The clerk paints your door, and pretends he saw nothing: all counted.

branches.title: Grave-shy
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The city's dead-cart rattles past the feast tables on its way to the gate, covered with a cloth. Go inside and shut the door until it has gone.

success.title: Until the cart has gone
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You stand in your dark hallway with your back to the door until the rattle has gone right down the street. When you come out again, the woman from next door is waiting.

"Are you ill?" she asks. "You went white as milk." She sounds kind. "[who:regard-neighbour]. I'm next door, if you ever need anything." While you were inside, the clerk painted your door: all counted.

cut-over-country.title: Cut-Over Country
cut-over-country.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The cut-over country: land the push cleared and gave up on. Stumps in rows for miles, a farmhouse with no roof.

In the stump field on the near bank a man stands watching the barges. His shirt is dark down one side, and his jaw hangs wrong. "That's one of them," someone behind you says. "Don't look it in the face."

It is the first risen you have ever seen. [who:regard-passenger] is at the rail beside you, gripping it with both hands.

branches.title: Keep looking
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Hold the rail and keep looking at it until it is out of sight. Put your other hand on her arm.

success.title: The passenger leans on you
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You watch it all the way to the bend. It turns its head to follow the barge, slowly, the whole time. Then the bend takes it.

[who:regard-passenger] lets out her breath and leans on you. "I thought I'd faint," she says. After a while she presses her bundle into your hands. "Keep this for me. If anything happens to me, keep it safe. Don't open it. Promise me."

It is light, and tied tight with string. She will not say what is in it.

failure.title: Shaken
failure.description:
PLACEHOLDER: It turns its head to follow the barge, and you are the one who looks away first. Your hands will not stop shaking on the rail.

"I'm frightened too," [who:regard-passenger] says quietly. Then, as if the fear has loosened something, she tells you why she is really going north: a thing she has told nobody on the barge, and makes you swear you will not repeat. When she has finished, she looks as if she wishes she had kept it.

branches.title: Look away, at the far bank
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Turn your back on it, and look at the far bank until it is gone. Leave her to watch it on her own.

success.title: Alone at the rail
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You fix your eyes on the far bank, on the stumps there, and count them until your heart slows. When you turn round again, the risen is gone behind the bend.

[who:regard-passenger] is still at the rail, white-faced. She watched it the whole way, alone. "You could have stayed," she says, without looking at you.

departure.title: Departure
departure.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The passengers queue along the landing to the plank of the first barge. At a table at the foot of the plank sits the convoy's tally-clerk: a thin man in a black coat, with ink on his fingers and a book in front of him as thick as a loaf. Every passenger, every sack and every ox that goes north goes into that book first. He writes slowly, and he does not hurry for anyone.

In front of you in the queue is a woman travelling alone. She holds one small bundle against her chest and watches the river as if it might change its mind. She has not said a word to anyone.

The queue shuffles forward. Something happens while you wait.

branches.title: Devout
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The parish priest is blessing the barges from the landing steps. Step out of the queue and kneel on the wet stones for his blessing, though you may lose your place.

success.title: Blessed for the road
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The priest's water is cold on your face. When you stand, the woman with the bundle is kneeling beside you, and the clerk has kept both your places.

"The river is long," he says, dipping his pen. "A blessing never hurt anyone's chances." He writes your name, then a word in the margin beside it. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk to the convoy. If you need anything counted, come to me."

The woman gets up off her knees. "[who:regard-passenger]," she says, and almost smiles. "I'll pray for the both of us, then."

branches.title: Doubter
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The priest flicks holy water at the barges from the steps. Say to the woman in front of you, just loud enough, that water never kept a barge afloat.

success.title: A low laugh
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The woman with the bundle laughs before she can stop herself, and covers her mouth. "Don't let him hear you," she whispers. "[who:regard-passenger]. I'll sit near you. You'll make the six weeks shorter."

The clerk heard you. He writes your name, then a word in the margin beside it, and looks up at you only once. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. The frontier has its own opinions about water, and about the dead. You'll hear them soon enough."

branches.title: Soft-hearted
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: At the back of the queue a small child is crying for someone left on the landing. Go back and crouch down, and talk to the child until the crying stops.

success.title: Until the child is quiet
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: It takes a while. You tell the child what the barges carry and how the oxen pull them, until the crying turns into questions. When the clerk calls your name you are the last to come to the table.

He is gentler with you than with the others. "That was kindly done. It's a long way to go frightened." He writes your name, and a word in the margin. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk to the convoy."

The woman with the bundle waited for you at the plank. "[who:regard-passenger]," she says. "I thought I was the only one who'd noticed the child."

branches.title: Hard-hearted
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A beggar works his way down the queue with his hand out, and stops in front of you. Push past him, and keep your coin in your pocket.

success.title: Nothing for him
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The beggar moves on to the woman with the bundle. She gives him a coin she clearly cannot spare, then gives you a long look.

"[who:regard-passenger]," she says at last, flatly, as if she is warning you. "We'll be neighbours for six weeks. We might as well know each other's names."

At the table the clerk writes you in without comment, then adds a word in the margin. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. Next."

branches.title: Proud
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: When your turn comes, the clerk asks your name without looking up from his book. Say nothing until he looks at you.

success.title: He looks up
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The silence goes on long enough that the queue behind you starts to mutter. At last the clerk lifts his head and looks at you properly.

"There," he says. "Now I've seen you. Name?" You give it. He writes it, and then writes a longer note in the margin than he has written for anyone else. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. I'll remember you, I think."

The woman with the bundle gives her name to him at once, and quietly to you on the plank: "[who:regard-passenger]. You'll make an enemy of him."

branches.title: Grasping
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: When your turn comes, ask the clerk what the crown paid for your passage, and what cargo rides in the barge you are going on.

success.title: Grain and nails
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He tells you, because nobody has asked him before and he knows the answer. "Grain, three hundred sacks. Iron nails for the Seal, twelve kegs. Your passage is a fifth of what one keg is worth." He writes your name, and a word in the margin beside it. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. You count like a merchant."

The woman with the bundle says she carries nothing worth counting. "[who:regard-passenger]," she adds. "In case you want to write me down too."

branches.title: Curious
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: While the clerk writes the man in front of you into his book, read the page upside down: the names above yours, and which barge each one is bound to.

success.title: Upside down
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You get through a dozen names before he notices. Most are going to the push with the levy. A few are marked with a small crown, and you cannot tell what it means. He turns the book away from you.

"It reads just as well the right way up," he says, writing your name and then a word in the margin. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. Nosy people last longer on the frontier, or much shorter."

The woman with the bundle asks, very quietly, what you saw. "[who:regard-passenger]," she adds. "Was my name there?"

branches.title: Loyal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The clerk tells the woman in front of you that this barge is full, and she will have to wait for the next one. Say that you will wait with her.

success.title: Room for two
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The clerk looks at the two of you for a long moment, then runs his pen down the page. "There's room for two if nobody brings a chair." He writes your names side by side, and a word in the margin beside yours. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. People who stick together are easier to count."

The woman grips your arm on the plank. "[who:regard-passenger]," she says. "Thank you. I didn't want to go alone."

branches.title: Hot-tempered
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A crewman pushes the queue back with a barge pole, and knocks the woman with the bundle off her feet into the mud. Shove him back, hard.

success.title: A shove for a shove
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The crewman goes down on his back in the mud. For a moment it looks like a fight, until the clerk stands up behind his table.

"Enough. Both of you." He does not raise his voice, and the crewman gets up and goes. The clerk sits, writes your name, and writes a long note in the margin beside it. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. I'll be watching the two of you for six weeks."

The woman wipes the mud off her bundle first, before her own hands. "[who:regard-passenger]," she says. "You didn't have to do that."

branches.title: Teetotal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A parting cup of ale comes down the queue from hand to hand, for luck on the river. Pass it on to the woman in front of you without drinking.

success.title: Your share, passed on
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She drinks her share and then yours, and wipes her mouth. "More luck for me, then," she says. "[who:regard-passenger]. I need all the luck there is."

The clerk saw the cup go past you. "A clear head is worth more than luck on this river," he says, writing your name and then a word in the margin. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk to the convoy."

branches.title: Hearty appetite
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The parish gives every passenger a loaf for the road. Eat yours while you stand in the queue, and ask the parish woman for another.

success.title: A second loaf
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The parish woman gives you the heel of another loaf and a look. The woman with the bundle laughs, breaks her own loaf in half and holds it out.

"You'll starve before the first waystation at this rate," she says. "[who:regard-passenger]. Take it. I can't eat when I'm nervous."

At the table the clerk writes your name and a word in the margin beside it. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. Rations are counted on this convoy. I'd go slower."

branches.title: Grave-shy
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A burial party carries a bier along the landing, up the steps to the old churchyard. Step back from the plank and look away until it has gone past, though you lose your place.

success.title: Until the bier has passed
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: Your skin crawls until the bier is up the steps and out of sight. When you look round, the woman with the bundle has stepped back with you.

"I don't like it either," she says. "Everyone says they lie quiet here. I still don't like it." She tells you her name: "[who:regard-passenger]."

The clerk writes you in last of all, with a word in the margin beside your name. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. The dead are nothing to be afraid of here. Up north is another matter."

getting-out.title: Getting Out

branches.title: Go back for the ox-boy
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go back into the deep water for the ox-boy, and drag him to the bank before the dead thing gets to him.

success.title: Out of the water
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You get him by the hair and then by the collar, and you kick and haul until your feet find gravel. The dead thing is coming. You drag him up out of the water onto the stones and keep dragging him, until the two of you are lying on the bank above the reeds, soaked and freezing, coughing up river.

He holds on to your arm and won't let go. "I'll pay you back," he says, over and over, shaking. "I'll pay you back, I swear it." He is twelve years old, and he has nothing.

failure.title: The river keeps him
failure.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You get him by the collar, and for a moment you have him. Then the current takes your feet from under you, and something in the water grabs your ankle and pulls, and you have to let go of him to fight it off.

When you come up, coughing, bleeding from a long scrape down your leg, he is gone. You look for him until someone drags you out onto the bank. You never see him again. You do not even know his name.

branches.title: Get yourself out
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Don't look back. Wade the last dozen strides to the bank and get yourself out of the water.

success.title: Dry ground
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You make yourself look at the bank and nothing else, and you wade until the water is at your knees, and then your ankles, and then you are on the stones, shaking all over.

When you do look back, the place where the ox-boy was is only water. Somebody else might have got to him. You tell yourself that somebody else might have got to him.

it-rises-on-the-barge.title: Under the Sacking
it-rises-on-the-barge.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: You jump the gap from the bank to the deck. The bargemen have backed away to the stern, and one of them has a boat-hook and is not using it.

The sacking slides off. [who:regard-partner] sits up on the grain sacks, very slowly, the way an old man gets out of bed. His chest is still the wrong shape. His eyes are open, and there is nobody in them. He turns his head toward the bargemen at the stern, toward the sound of them, and starts to get up.

"He's yours," the bargeman with the boat-hook says to you, and his voice cracks. "You brought him aboard. You do it."

branches.title: Put it down with the boat-hook
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take the boat-hook out of the bargeman's hands, and put your partner down yourself, before he reaches them.

success.title: Put down
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He comes at you instead of them, faster than you thought a broken man could move. The hook takes him in the chest and he keeps coming, up the shaft, and his hands close on your arm and his teeth close on your shoulder. You get him down on the deck, and you hold him there with your whole weight, and you shout for the bargemen to get the clerk.

It takes a long time. At the halt [who:regard-clerk] seals what is left, with the prayers, while a hauler binds up your shoulder. "You held him," the clerk says. "Most would have let go." He enters the nail in his book.

branches.title: Heave it over the side
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Get behind him and heave him over the side into the river, where he cannot reach anyone on the barge.

success.title: Into the river
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You put your shoulder into his back and heave, and he goes over the side with hardly a splash. The current takes him at once. For a moment you see his face turned up toward you under the brown water, and then he is gone downriver, toward the country you came through.

The bargemen do not thank you. Nobody is hurt, and nobody says it was wrong. But at the halt the haulers hear what you did, and they look at the river, and then at you. He is out there now, in the water, and he will not stop.

night-in-the-city.title: Night in the City
night-in-the-city.intro: {if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: The night after the rider came back. The streets are empty by dark, and the watch go past your door twice before midnight. Nobody in the city sleeps well. Through the wall you can hear the family next door, awake too, talking in low voices. A dog barks for an hour somewhere near the gate and then stops very suddenly.{else}PLACEHOLDER: The night after the rider came back, with the gate shut and the district on the wrong side of it. The watch walk the top of the wall above you all night with torches, looking outward, toward the river road. Nobody in the lean-tos sleeps well. Out on the burning ground, the night fires are burning again, and there are more of them than yesterday.{/if}

branches.title: Wake
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Wake to another grey morning, and whatever it brings.

success.title: A heavy sleep
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You fall asleep all at once, heavily, as if you had been knocked down, and wake in the morning with no dreams and no feeling in you at all. It is a relief, for now. Outside, people are already queueing for bread. The price has gone up again overnight, so you buy less than you meant to, and you are hungry before you have finished eating it.

success.title: Nightmares
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Nightmares all night: a horse with no rider, walking up the road toward you in the dark, and the dead walking beside it, keeping step. You wake again and again with your heart pounding. In the morning the bread has gone up again overnight, so you buy less than you meant to, and you are hungry before you have finished eating it.

night-on-the-bank.title: Night on the Bank
night-on-the-bank.intro: PLACEHOLDER: The first night after the ford. The survivors sleep on the far bank in the reeds, with the barges that crossed tied up beside them and the escort's pickets all round, facing the trees. Nobody lets the fires go down. Out in the dark, in the ford, something is still moving in the water, and every so often a splash makes the whole camp go quiet.{if [q:prologue-pulled-someone-out] > 0} The ox-boy you pulled out has crept in next to you, and sleeps with one hand holding your sleeve.{/if}{if [q:prologue-lost-someone-in-the-ford] > 0} Every time you close your eyes, you feel the boy's collar slip out of your hand.{/if}

branches.title: Wake
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Wake up on the far bank, in the grey light, to the sound of the sergeants getting the survivors moving.

success.title: A heavy sleep
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You sleep as if someone had hit you with a club, and you do not dream at all. When they wake you at first light, it takes you a long moment to remember where you are and what happened. When you do remember, you feel nothing. It is as if it happened to somebody else. The barges are already being loaded for the last day's haul to the city.

success.title: Nightmares
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You dream of the ford all night. The water, the ropes going slack, the dead standing up out of the river one after another, all together, and walking toward you in a line. Every time you wake, the splashing out in the dark is still going on. At first light, the sergeants get everyone moving for the last day's haul to the city, and you are glad to go.

no-walls-tonight.title: No Walls Tonight
no-walls-tonight.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: At dusk the convoy reaches the last waystation before the ford, and it is dark: no lamps, no smoke, the gate open. The escort captain looks in and rides back. "Nobody goes in. We camp on the bank."

So tonight nobody has walls. The escort want a watch line out past the firelight, facing the trees, and a sergeant is walking the bank looking for haulers to stand it. He stops in front of you.

branches.title: Keep watch
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take a spear from the sergeant, and stand the watch out on the line, in the cold, facing the trees.

success.title: Shapes on the treeline
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: For hours there is nothing but wind and the river. Then, near midnight, something moves along the treeline: shapes, many of them, keeping to the edge of the trees, all going the same way. North. Upriver. Toward the ford.

"Did you see that?" whispers the soldier next to you. You both watch until they are gone. You cannot tell if they were the dead or men. They made no sound at all.

When the next watch comes out to take over, you are frozen through. Your coat is rolled up in the pack on your back, and you never once thought to put it on.

branches.title: Sleep close to the fire
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Tell the sergeant you pulled all day, and go back to the fire to sleep while you can.

success.title: Warm, but
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He lets you go with a look. You lie down as close to the fire as you can get, and sleep like a dropped stone.

The fire dies before dawn and you wake up shaking, with frost on your blanket. Your coat is still rolled up in your pack. When you open the pack to get it out, the food you had saved is gone. Someone took it in the night, while the whole camp slept around you, and nobody saw who.

six-weeks-upriver.title: Six Weeks Upriver
six-weeks-upriver.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The heartland goes by slowly, then all at once. For the first days there are walled towns on the bank, ferries, church towers, and people who wave at the barges from the fields. Then the towns stop. The crown licenses no farms along the middle river, so there is nobody to wave.

After that, the days have one shape. At dawn the tally-clerk walks the deck with his book and counts everyone, and every morning the count is the same. The haulers lean into the ropes on the towpath and the barge creeps north against the current. Every night the convoy reaches a walled waystation and ties up under its guns, and the haulers light their fires on the open bank outside the walls.{if [q:prologue-left-because-levy] > 0} The levy men sleep in a pen of their own, and a guard counts them twice.{/if}{if [q:prologue-left-because-someone] > 0} You read the last letter again every night, until the folds start to tear.{/if}{if [q:prologue-left-because-crime] > 0} Every time an escort rider comes alongside, you wait for someone to say your name.{/if}

[who:regard-passenger] sleeps on the next sacks to yours in the hold. You learn how she takes her bread, and that she talks in her sleep, but not what she is going north for.

The weather turns. The mornings come up grey, and the wind off the water gets into your clothes. The land changes too. The woods come back, and then, around a bend, the woods stop again, and there is nothing but stumps.

branches.title: Go up on deck
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Climb up out of the hold, and see where you are.

success.title: The north
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You climb up on deck into the grey morning.

talk-clerk.title: A Word with the Tally-Clerk
talk-clerk.intro: {if [q:prologue] >= 8}PLACEHOLDER: [who:regard-clerk] is sitting on a coil of rope with his bad leg stretched out in front of him and a crutch beside it. His hands keep moving to where the manifest chest used to be, and finding nothing. "Sit," he says. "I've nothing to count. I might as well talk."{else}PLACEHOLDER: [who:regard-clerk] blots his page, closes the manifest on a ribbon to keep his place, and folds his inky hands on top of it. "Well?" he says. "I have a few minutes before the evening count. Ask."{/if}

branches.title: Ask what he wrote in the margin beside your name
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask him what he wrote in the margin of the manifest, beside your name, the day you came aboard.

success.title: A word
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He does not open the book. "A word," he says. "I write a word beside every passenger. It helps me remember who is who, six weeks on." He looks at you over his folded hands. "Yours isn't a bad word, if that's what you're worried about."

You ask him what it is. He smiles very slightly. "If I told people their words, they would all start behaving like them. Or trying not to. Either way my book would be wrong." That is all he will say about it.

branches.title: Ask him why he docks the slow
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask him why he docks a hauler a day's wage for being slow, when the barge-masters never complain.

success.title: A finger a day
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: "Because the barge-masters don't know how to count," he says. He opens the manifest at the back, where there is a page of numbers in columns. "This is the depth at the ford, every year for thirty years, from the clerks before me. It falls a finger's width every day after the harvest. This year it was low before we even started." He taps the last column. "Every day we're late, the water drops another finger. One slow hauler costs the whole convoy an hour. Enough slow haulers, and we reach the ford and can't cross it." He closes the book. "So I dock them. Nobody likes me for it. That isn't my job."

branches.title: Ask him what rides in the charter chest
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask him what is in the chest the escort guard day and night: the charter, and whatever comes with it.

success.title: Names
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He lowers his voice, though there is nobody near. "The king's charter for the frontier, under seal. And with it, the things it promises." He counts them off on his inky fingers. "The new roll of citizens for the city: every name to be added to the count. Land grants beyond the walls, signed and sealed. Appointments to the new offices." He looks at you. "Names. The chest is full of names. Somebody's whole future, a few hundred times over."

"And every one of them is in here too," he adds, and puts his hand flat on the manifest. "If the charter went in the river tomorrow, this book would be the only list of what it promised, and to whom."

branches.title: Ask him about the waystation ahead
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask him about the last waystation before the ford, where the convoy will stop tonight.

success.title: No runner
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He frowns, and it is the first time you have seen him look uncertain. "Every year, the keeper sends a boy down the towpath to meet us, two days out, with his tally: how many beds, how much fodder, what the river's doing at the ford. It's in the rules. It's been done that way for thirty years."

He turns a page, and back again. "No boy this year. Not yesterday, not today." He shuts the book. "Probably the boy is sick. Probably the keeper is lazy. I'll have words with him tonight." He does not sound as if he believes it.

branches.title: Ask him what he saw at the ford
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask him what he saw at the ford, from the stern of his barge in the middle of it all.

success.title: Before anything
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He has clearly told this before, to people who did not listen. "The ropes were cut," he says. "Before anything came out of the water. I had the end of mine in my hand, and it was cut clean, and I was still looking at it when the fires went up on the bank." He rubs his bad leg. "Then the dead. Then something in the water took my leg, and I never saw it. I never saw what did it."

"The escort say it was raiders. The crews say it was the dead. They're both right, and neither of them wants to hear it. Somebody cut those ropes first." He looks at you. "Somebody planned it. The dead don't plan."

branches.title: Ask him about the manifest
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask him about the manifest, and the council's men who took it from him at the gate.

success.title: Every name
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: His mouth goes thin. "Every sack of grain. Every keg of nails. Every name on the roll, every grant, every appointment, every passenger who went into that river. All of it, in my hand, for six weeks." He looks at the city wall. "They didn't count the wounded. They didn't ask who was dead. They counted the chest. Two of them, in the council's colours, with a paper I wasn't allowed to read."

"Whoever has that book," he says, "knows exactly what was lost, and who it belonged to. And knows who doesn't know." He does not say anything else for a while.

branches.title: Ask him what became of the escort captain
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask him what he knows of the escort captain, and what happened to him at the ford.

success.title: The captain
success.description: {if [q:prologue-captain-fate]==2}PLACEHOLDER: "Alive," he says. "Somewhere inside, telling the council it was raiders. He's telling it very loudly, I hear." He shifts his leg. "He sent a man to me this morning to ask whether my book said anything about his orders at the ford. I said my book says what happened. He didn't like that."{else}PLACEHOLDER: "Nobody's found him," he says. "His horse came out. He didn't." He is quiet for a moment. "He was a hard man and a fair one, and he knew fords. He went into that one as if he knew what was waiting. I keep thinking about that." He writes nothing down. There is nothing to write in.{/if}

branches.title: Thank him for pulling you out of the ford
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Thank him for pulling you out of the ford by the collar, and for not letting go when something took his leg.

success.title: Thanks
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He looks embarrassed, which you did not know he could. "You were in my manifest," he says. "I don't like losing people from it. It spoils the count." Then, after a moment, more quietly: "You're welcome. I'd do it again. I'd rather not have to."

He holds out his hand, inky even now, and you shake it.

branches.title: Leave him to his work
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Say goodbye, and leave him in peace.

success.title: Back to his book
success.description: {if [q:prologue] >= 8}PLACEHOLDER: He nods, and goes back to looking at the wall, and the place where his chest used to be.{else}PLACEHOLDER: He nods, opens the manifest at the ribbon, and goes back to his columns before you are off the barge.{/if}

talk-priestess.title: A Word with the Priestess
talk-priestess.intro: PLACEHOLDER: [who:regard-priestess] finishes the line she is writing, wipes her pen, and turns on her stool to face you. "Go on," she says. "The dead will wait a few minutes. They're good at it."

branches.title: Ask her about your neighbour
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask her about [who:regard-neighbour], and the family next door.

success.title: The neighbour
success.description: {if [q:prologue-first-death-city-paid] > 0}PLACEHOLDER: "The husband came to see me," she says. "To ask how much you paid, so he could write it down and pay you back. I told him." She looks at you. "He'll try. He won't manage it, and he'll hate that more than he'd ever hate you. Be kind to him about it, if you can."{else}{if [q:prologue-first-death-city-burned] > 0}PLACEHOLDER: "She went on the cart at noon, and the fire that night," she says, without any expression at all. "The husband walked behind the cart all the way to the burning ground. They usually do." She turns back to her book, and then turns round again. "At least you came to ask. Most people who stand by don't."{else}PLACEHOLDER: "Sealed and buried in the paupers' ground, with a stone," she says. "The children can visit her. That's worth something." She lowers her voice. "You were right to push me. The church's price is a sin. I just can't say so out loud."{/if}{/if}

branches.title: Ask her about the old woman from the next lean-to
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask her about the grandmother from the lean-to next to yours, and what became of her.

success.title: The grandmother
success.description: {if [q:prologue-first-death-outside-helped] > 0}PLACEHOLDER: "I heard," she says. "A burning outside the rite, in the ditch behind the lean-tos. The watch were very pleased with themselves." She shrugs. "Burned is burned. She won't rise. I've seen what happens to the ones who wait for the cart and don't get sealed." She dips her pen. "I didn't say that. You didn't hear it."{else}{if [q:prologue-first-death-outside-priestess] > 0}PLACEHOLDER: "She went to the fire whole, with the prayers said," she says. "The family haven't forgiven either of us for it." She rubs her eyes. "They wanted their own fire, their own words. I understand it better than they think. But I can't stop the city's sentence, and I won't let anyone go to it without the Seal if I can help it."{else}{if [q:prologue-first-death-outside-reported] > 0}PLACEHOLDER: "The watch brought her in on the cart," she says. "I sealed her before she went to the fire, since nobody else was going to." She looks at you steadily. "The sergeant says you're very helpful. He says it like a compliment." She goes back to her writing.{else}PLACEHOLDER: "Old women die in the cold every winter out there," she says. "I write them all down." She turns a page. "Most of them, nobody asks about."{/if}{/if}{/if}

branches.title: Ask her who reads the register of the dead
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask her what she writes in the register of the dead, and who reads it.

success.title: The long pages
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She turns the huge book round so you can see it. "Every death in the city and the district," she says. "Name, if there is one. Where, and when, and what of. Whether sealed or burned." She turns a thick block of pages. "These are the counted. The council reads these, because the counted pay taxes." She turns a much thicker block. "And these are the uncounted. Nobody reads these."

"They get longer every year," she says. "Much longer. Faster than the other pages." She closes the book. "I send the council the numbers every quarter. Nobody has ever written back."

branches.title: Ask her why she pays for other people's rites
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask her quietly why she pays out of her own purse for the rites of people who can't.

success.title: Somebody has to
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: For a moment you think she will deny it. Then she sighs. "Because somebody has to, and I'm the one standing there when the money runs out. Because a child shouldn't have to watch their mother go on the cart for want of a coin." She shrugs. "Because the prayers might matter. Nobody knows. I'd rather not find out the hard way."

"Don't tell anyone," she adds. "The church would call it undercutting its price. They'd send me somewhere I couldn't do it."

branches.title: Ask her if she has heard anything about the rider
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask her if she has heard anything about the rider who came back alone, and what he said.

success.title: Sent away
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She puts her pen down. "They sent for me at dusk," she says. "To the councillor's house where they took him. A servant came running and said bring your bag. So I brought it." She is quiet for a moment. "I got as far as the hall. Then a man in the council's colours came down the stairs and said I wasn't needed after all, and gave me a coin for my trouble, and showed me out."

"You don't send for the death-watch unless someone is dying," she says. "And you don't send her away unless you don't want her to see who."

branches.title: Ask her about the dead who are still lying at the ford
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask her about the dead who are still lying in the ford, and on the banks, where nobody has sealed them.

success.title: Nobody has gone
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: "Hundreds," she says. "Passengers, haulers, escort. Lying in the water and on the gravel, with nobody to seal them or burn them." She does not look at you. "Every one of them will get up. Some already have, most likely."

"I asked the bishop's clerk for a boat and six men to go down and do what can be done. He said the council hasn't decided what to send yet. Not until they know what's out there." She picks up her pen and puts it down again. "Someone should go. Someone with a reason."

branches.title: Let her get back to her register
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Thank her, and let her get back to the register.

success.title: Back to the register
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: She nods, and turns back to the register, and is writing again before you have reached the door.

the-barge-swings-wide.title: The Barge Swings Wide
the-barge-swings-wide.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The next day, on the haul toward the ford, the river narrows and the current doubles. Out on the water, your barge catches it wrong and swings wide. The rope goes from slack to iron in a heartbeat and jerks the whole line sideways toward the water.

Most of you go down on the clay and hold on. [who:regard-partner] is on the edge of the path. The rope takes him off his feet and over the bank, and he goes into the river between the bank and the barge.

It takes six of you to haul him out. By then the barge has swung back and caught him against the bank. You lay him on the towpath. He is grey, and there is river water coming out of his mouth, and something is wrong with the shape of his chest.

He finds your sleeve. {if [q:prologue-owed-the-partner] > 0}"You owe me, remember," he says, and tries to laugh, and can't. "Pay it to my mother. Lower bank. Anyone can tell you where."{else}{if [q:regard-partner] >= 1}"Don't let them leave me on the bank," he says. "Not for the crows. Not for the other thing." He holds on hard. "Promise."{else}"Tell the clerk I finished the haul," he whispers. "Tell him not to dock me." His eyes go past you, to the sky.{/if}{/if}

The escort sergeant rides up while the haulers are still standing round him. "Is he dead?" he asks. Somebody says, "Not yet." The sergeant looks down the line at the barges waiting. "When he is, get the line moving. The convoy doesn't stop." A few minutes later, he is.

branches.title: Kneel by him on the bank
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Kneel on the wet towpath beside him, and close his eyes.

success.title: He is gone
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You close his eyes.

the-body-rises.title: At Dusk
the-body-rises.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: You keep watch beside the sail all afternoon. Nobody else will sit near it. The light goes, and the crew hang a lantern from the awning pole, and further along the deck a woman who has been awake for two nights falls asleep sitting up, with her child in her lap.

Some time after dark, the sail moves.

It is only a little at first, a twitch, as if a cat were underneath. Then the whole shape sits up with the canvas still over its face, and turns its head toward the sleeping woman, and starts to crawl.

Someone screams. The crew are running. [who:regard-clerk] is shouting for the mallet. The thing under the sail is faster than you would believe, and the woman and her child are between it and the rail.

branches.title: Get between her and the sleeper
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Throw yourself in front of the sleeping woman and her child, and hold it off until the crew get there.

success.title: Between them
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You get your arms around it and it turns on you instead. Its fingers find your arm through the canvas and close like a trap, and its teeth close on your sleeve and then through it. You hold on. You do not know how long.

Then the crew are on it, four of them, and the clerk kneels on its chest and drives the nail in with the mallet, once, twice, three times, until it stops. The woman is up against the rail with her child, screaming. They are not hurt.

Your arm is bleeding badly. "Now you know," the clerk says, out of breath, tying his handkerchief round it. "Now you know why we don't wait."

branches.title: Take the nail from the clerk, and do it yourself
branches.description: {if [q:trait]==12}PLACEHOLDER: You cannot make yourself touch it. Your hands will not do it.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Snatch the nail-bag and the mallet out of the clerk's hands, and finish what you stopped him doing.{/if}

success.title: Too late for waiting
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You get the nail out of the bag as it reaches you. It catches your wrist and pulls, stronger than any living woman, and you go down on the deck with it on top of you. The canvas slips off its face, and it is her face, and it is not.

You put the point above the ear, where the clerk was going to put it that afternoon, and you hit it with the mallet, and hit it again, until it stops moving. Then you sit on the deck and look at the blood on your wrist.

"That's the way of it," the clerk says, very quietly. "You learn it once." He takes the mallet out of your hand.

the-bond.title: The Bond
the-bond.intro: PLACEHOLDER: You close your eyes and try to picture them clearly, the way they were the last time: their face, their hands, their voice saying your name. It is harder than it should be. Distance does that.{if [q:bond]==9} You have never seen this one's face at all, only their handwriting. You picture them anyway.{/if}

branches.title: A woman
branches.description: {if [q:bond]==9}PLACEHOLDER: The letters say she is a woman. Picture her from the letters: the round, careful hand she writes in, and the things she chose to tell you and the things she didn't.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Picture her: her face in the firelight, the way she stood, and the way she said your name.{/if}

success.title: Her face
success.description: {if [q:bond]==9}PLACEHOLDER: You give her a face in your mind: kind, a little plain, with ink on her fingers from all those letters. It is probably wrong. She is out there on the river somewhere tonight, in the dark, coming toward you. You hold on to the picture until sleep comes.{else}PLACEHOLDER: She is out there somewhere tonight, under the same dark, and you do not know if she is thinking of you too. You keep her face in your mind, as clear as you can make it, until sleep comes and takes it.{/if}

branches.title: A man
branches.description: {if [q:bond]==9}PLACEHOLDER: The letters say he is a man. Picture him from the letters: the stiff, upright hand he writes in, and the things he chose to tell you and the things he didn't.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Picture him: his face in the firelight, the way he stood, and the way he said your name.{/if}

success.title: His face
success.description: {if [q:bond]==9}PLACEHOLDER: You give him a face in your mind: serious, a little stern, with ink on his fingers from all those letters. It is probably wrong. He is out there on the river somewhere tonight, in the dark, coming toward you. You hold on to the picture until sleep comes.{else}PLACEHOLDER: He is out there somewhere tonight, under the same dark, and you do not know if he is thinking of you too. You keep his face in your mind, as clear as you can make it, until sleep comes and takes it.{/if}

the-characters-house.title: Your House
the-characters-house.intro: PLACEHOLDER: Your house: two rooms and a loft, in a street of houses just like it, pressed shoulder to shoulder inside the walls. The count is painted on the door. Inside there is a hearth, a bed, a chest with your things in it, and a shelf with what food you have.{if [q:hunger] >= 3} The shelf looks emptier every time you look at it.{/if}{if [q:cold] >= 3} The hearth is cold, and the cold has got into the walls.{/if}

branches.title: Eat from your provisions
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take something down from the shelf, and sit at your own table to eat it.

success.title: A meal
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Bread from the baker at the corner, a little dripping, an onion, and small beer from the jug. You eat at your own table with the door shut and the street noise outside. It is not a feast, but it is yours, and it fills you.

branches.title: Lie down for the night
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Bar the door, bank the fire, and go to bed.

success.title: Night falls
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You bar the door, which you never used to bother to do. Outside, the watch goes past more often than usual, and somewhere down the street someone is crying. You lie in the dark and listen to the city, and think about the rider, until sleep comes.

the-clerk-catches-up.title: The Tally-Clerk Catches Up

branches.title: Tell him exactly what you saw
branches.description: {if [q:origin]==1}PLACEHOLDER: Tell him all of it: the stump field, the dark shirt, the jaw, the way it turned its head to follow the barge.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Tell him what you saw: the end of the rope was cut, clean and square, as if with one stroke of an axe.{/if}

success.title: Written down
success.description: {if [q:origin]==1}PLACEHOLDER: He writes while you talk, and asks you to say the part about its head again. Then he blots the page. "Thank you. That is the third this week, and all on the east bank. Last year I saw none this far south." He looks up the river, toward the north. "I don't like it when the numbers change."{else}PLACEHOLDER: He writes it down and underlines it. "Cut," he says. "Not chafed through." He is quiet for a moment. "There is nobody upriver of us who should be cutting ropes. The convoy is the only traffic going north, and the rafts don't use tow-ropes." He closes the book. "Thank you. I'd rather know than guess."{/if}

branches.title: Ask him why he wants to know
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask him why a tally-clerk cares what anybody saw.

success.title: For the other end
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He looks at you as if the answer is obvious. "Because the council at the other end will ask me what we saw on the way. They always ask. I would rather give them numbers than stories." He taps the book. "Everything goes in here: what we carry, who we carry, and what the river shows us. It's the only true account there will be."

You tell him what you saw, in the end. He writes it down without comment, and you have the feeling you have been counted too.

branches.title: Tell him you didn't see anything
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Shrug, and tell him you didn't see anything worth writing down.

success.title: Saw nothing
success.description: {if [q:origin]==1}PLACEHOLDER: He writes something short beside your name. "Six people at that rail," he says, "and not one of them saw anything. Remarkable." He moves on along the deck without looking back.{else}PLACEHOLDER: He writes something short beside your name. "A rope as long as a barge floats past the whole line, and nobody saw it. Remarkable." He moves on up the towpath without looking back.{/if}

the-cold-night.title: The Cold Night
the-cold-night.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The frost comes down hard in the night. Some time before dawn, the father of the family scratches at the sacking of your lean-to. "It's the old woman," he whispers. "Please. My wife says you know what to do."

In their lean-to the grandmother is lying on all the blankets the family owns, with the children packed round her to keep her warm. It isn't working. Her breath rattles, and her hands are like ice. She has not been on anybody's count for thirty years.

When she sees you, she beckons you down close. Her voice is a thread. {if [q:trait]==1}"You pray," she says. "I heard you. Say one for me. And then don't let the city have me. Promise."{else}"Don't let them take me to their fires," she says. "The watch. The city. I've seen what they do. Let my own people do it, the old way, with the right words." Her fingers close on your sleeve. "Promise me."{/if}

She dies as the sky gets grey, very quietly. For a moment nobody moves. Then the mother starts, without a word, to gather wood.

"She's not going on their cart," the father says. "We'll burn her ourselves. Now, before the watch comes round." He looks at you. "Are you with us?"

branches.title: Stay with the family
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stay kneeling beside her in the cold, with the family, while the sky gets light.

success.title: Before light
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You stay with them while the sky gets light.

the-crisis-begins.title: The Crisis Begins
the-crisis-begins.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: Morning comes up grey over the city. The bells ring for Prime as if it were an ordinary day. At the river gate the survivors are still camped on the quay, waiting for someone to count them. At the land gate the death-house yard is full. The night fires are still smoking on the burning ground.

The council has still not said what happens now. But the bakers have put their prices up again, and the watch are on every corner, and people are talking in low voices about the winter.

Everyone is deciding where to be when it comes. So are you.

branches.title: Go inside the walls
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go back inside the walls, where your door has your count painted on it.

success.title: Inside the walls
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You walk back up through the streets to your own door, with the count painted on it, and it has never looked so thin. Counted. Whatever that is worth, with the winter's grain lying in the ford, you are about to find out. Around you, the city is starting to count everything: the bread, the grain, the people. You are on the right side of the count, for now.

branches.title: Go outside the walls
branches.description: {if [q:counted]==2}PLACEHOLDER: Go back out through the land gate to the district against the wall, where you are half-counted, and where you belong.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Go out through the gate to the district against the wall, where the uncounted live, since the city has no room for you inside.{/if}

success.title: Outside the walls
success.description: {if [q:counted]==2}PLACEHOLDER: The gate shuts behind you. Half-counted: near enough to the walls to feel safe, not near enough to be safe. When the city starts counting its bread, you know which pages of the register you will be on. The night fires are still smoking. It is going to be a long winter out here.{else}PLACEHOLDER: The watch point you out through the gate with the other uncounted from the convoy, and it shuts behind you. Out here, among the lean-tos against the wall, nobody counts you, and nobody feeds you. When the city starts counting its bread, you will not be on any page. It is going to be a long winter.{/if}

the-death-house.title: The Death-House
the-death-house.intro: PLACEHOLDER: A narrow stone house set into the tower of the land gate, with one door inside the wall and one outside. Every death in the city and the district is written down here, and the city's cart leaves from its yard for the night fires.{if [q:presence-priestess]==2} Today the yard is full of the dead from the ford, under sheets, and the door is shut. Through the window you can see [who:regard-priestess] moving from one to the next with her nail-bag.{else} [who:regard-priestess] sits at a high desk under the window, writing in the register of the dead, with her nail-bag on a hook beside her.{/if}

branches.title: Talk to the death-watch priestess
branches.description: {if [q:presence-priestess]==2}PLACEHOLDER: She is busy with the dead from the ford, and the door is shut. It will be hours before she is finished.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Stand by her desk, and talk to her while she writes.{/if}

success.title: A word with the priestess
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You stand by her desk.

the-empty-berths.title: The Empty Berths
the-empty-berths.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: Evening at the docks below the rapids. The convoy's berths stand empty, as they have all week, and the river is empty to the bend.

[who:regard-neighbour] has come down to watch for it too, with a shawl over her head, and a cough she did not have last week. "My husband says it's the low water," she says. "It's always the low water, when things are late."

branches.title: Wait at the docks for the convoy
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stay at the docks until dark, and watch the river for the first barge.

success.title: Buying early
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: No barge comes. [who:regard-neighbour] goes home to her children, coughing. You stay.

As the light goes, you notice you are not the only one watching. Along the quay, men in good coats are going in and out of the grain warehouses with clerks and lanterns, and carts are being loaded. They are buying up the grain that is left in the city, early, at today's price. Someone expects tomorrow's price to be higher.

By full dark you are cold through. Your coat is over your arm, where it has been all evening, and you never thought to put it on.

branches.title: Go home
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Walk home with [who:regard-neighbour] before it gets dark, and let her talk.

success.title: A rumour
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She talks the whole way, the way people do when they are worried. At your doors she lowers her voice. "My husband heard something at the mills. There's a man on the council who wants the convoy late. Wants it very late." She will not say who. "Maybe it's nothing," she says, and coughs, and goes in.

Your house is cold. The fire has gone out, and your coat is still over your arm, not on your back.

the-far-bank.title: The Far Bank
the-far-bank.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: By late afternoon it is over, or it has stopped. Nobody is sure which.

The survivors are on the far bank, in a long ragged camp among the reeds: the people from maybe twenty barges out of a hundred, and whatever they carried out of the water. Out in the ford, barges lie on their sides on the gravel bars, and some of them are burning. On the near bank, far off, the barges that never went in are still tied up, with their people standing on the decks, looking across. Nobody knows yet whether they will cross tomorrow, or turn back.

{if [q:prologue-captain-fate]==2}The escort captain is alive. He walks up and down the camp with his arm strapped across his chest, setting pickets, and he will not sit down.{else}The escort captain's horse came out of the ford on its own, with an empty saddle. Nobody saw him go down. A sergeant has taken command, and he looks as if he would rather be anywhere else.{/if}

[who:regard-clerk] is lying on a door somebody pulled off a barge, with his leg wrapped in a shirt that is soaked red. The manifest chest is beside him. He has one hand on it, even now.

Everyone is talking at once, and no two people tell it the same way.

branches.title: Listen to the escort
