branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go over to the escort soldiers round their fire, and listen to what they say happened.

success.title: Raiders
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: "Raiders," says a corporal with a bandaged head, and the others nod. "Free people, from the forest. They lit fires on the bank to blind us, and they were in the trees with bows, waiting for us to string out. They know this ford better than we do." He spits into the fire. "The dead? The dead were just the dead. There's always dead in a ford. Bad luck they came up when they did." Nobody around the fire says anything about the dead after that.

branches.title: Listen to the barge crews
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Sit down with the barge crews, who saw it all from their decks, and listen to them.

success.title: The dead
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: "They came up out of the water," says a bargewoman, with her hands wrapped round a cup she isn't drinking. "All at once. In a line. Like soldiers on a parade ground. I've seen the dead in the river all my life, and they don't do that. They don't walk together." Her husband tells her to hush, and she won't. "Something made them. Something drove them at us. You ask anyone who was on a deck." They all nod. Nobody on the decks saw any raiders.

branches.title: Listen to the haulers
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go to the haulers' fire and listen to them, since they were in the water on the ropes when it started.

success.title: Someone drove them
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: "The ropes went first," says an old hauler. "Before anything. Every rope on the line went slack at once, and I pulled mine in, and it was cut. Somebody in the water, cutting." Nobody saw who.

Then a young hauler with a burnt hand leans in. "There was a man," she says. "On the far bank, above the fires. Just standing there with his arms up, like this, like a drover moving cattle. And the dead came on." The old man tells her she's seeing things. "It was magic," she says. "I know what I saw." Nobody else saw him.

branches.title: Help carry the tally-clerk up the bank
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take one end of the door the clerk is lying on, and help carry him up the bank away from the water.

success.title: The ropes were cut
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He is feverish, and he talks all the way up the bank, gripping the chest with one hand. "Cut," he says. "Tell them it was cut. I had the end of the rope in my hand before anything came out of the water. Clean, like a knife through butter. Before anything." He catches your sleeve. "Nobody will believe a clerk. Write it down. Somebody write it down."

At the top of the bank they put him under a sailcloth with the other wounded. He is still talking about the rope when you leave him, and now he doesn't know who he is talking to.

the-fellow-passenger-dies.title: The Nail
the-fellow-passenger-dies.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: Nobody on the frontier waits. Two of the crew come under the awning, kneel, and take hold of her arms, and they are not gentle about it. [who:regard-clerk] comes behind them with his book and a leather bag.

He opens the manifest on his knee, finds her name, and writes beside it: one nail. Only then does he take the nail out of the bag. It is as long as your hand, black iron, with a square head. A crewman holds out a mallet.

"Hold her head," the clerk says. "Turn it to the side."

"We don't do it like this at home," someone says. It takes you a moment to understand it was you. At home the dead lie in the church for a night, and a priest comes with candles and prayers, and they stay in the ground. Here the clerk is looking at you, waiting, with the nail in his hand.

"This isn't home," he says. "Well?"

branches.title: Stop them, and wait for a priest in the city
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Put your hand on the clerk's wrist. Tell him to wait: there will be a priest in the city, and she should have one, as she would at home.

success.title: The nail goes back in the bag
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The crewmen look at the clerk. The clerk looks at you for a long moment, then at the body.

"It's two days to the city," he says. "Maybe three. She won't wait that long." But he puts the nail back in the bag, and draws a line through what he wrote. "It's your conscience. I'll write that too." The crewmen let go of her arms and wipe their hands on their trousers. One of them spits over the side. They will remember whose idea this was.

You wrap her in the sail yourself, and sit down beside her to keep watch.

branches.title: Let them seal it
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take your hand away. Stand back, and watch them seal her here and now.

success.title: The nail
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The clerk says a prayer so fast it is one long word. He sets the point of the nail above her ear and strikes it once, twice. The sound is small and flat. It is over quicker than you thought it could be.

You make yourself watch every part of it: where he puts the point, how hard he strikes, what the crew do with their hands. You will need to know.

Then he opens the manifest again and draws a neat line through her name. "Deceased, sealed," he says as he writes it. "Half a day south of the ford." He closes the book.

branches.title: Do it yourself
branches.description: {if [q:trait]==12}PLACEHOLDER: You cannot make yourself go near the body, let alone put a nail in it. Someone else will have to do it.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Hold out your hand for the nail and the mallet. She was your friend on this barge. If it has to be done, you will do it.{/if}

success.title: Your hand on the nail
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The clerk hesitates, then gives you the nail. "Above the ear," he says quietly. "Hard. Don't stop halfway."

It takes two blows. The first one is not hard enough, and you feel it in your teeth. The second one is. The crew let go of her arms.

The clerk nods to you once, and enters the nail in the manifest in his neat hand. "Not many would," he says. The other passengers were watching from the far end of the deck. For the rest of the day, none of them will stand near you.

the-fever.title: The Fever
the-fever.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The fever comes on in the night, after the cold hours moored off the dark waystation. By morning [who:regard-passenger] is burning and shivering at once, and the air in the hold is too thick for her. Two of the crew help you carry her up on deck, and you lay her on a folded sail under the awning, out of the wind.

The barge moves on toward the ford. You wet a cloth in the river and hold it to her face. For a while she talks about ordinary things: her mother's kitchen, a dog she had once, whether the city has proper bread.

Around noon she goes quiet, and then she finds your hand.

{if [q:passengers-bundle] > 0}"You've still got it?" she whispers. "The bundle. Don't open it. Take it to the city. Someone will know what it means. Promise me." You promise. Her grip loosens.{else}{if [q:prologue-passengers-secret] > 0}"What I told you," she whispers. "At the rail. Don't tell them. Not the clerk, not anyone. Let it go in the river with me." You promise. Her grip loosens.{else}"You looked away," she whispers, "that day at the rail. I don't blame you. Stay now, though. I don't want to be on my own for this part." You stay. Her grip loosens.{/if}{/if}

A little after noon, with the sun on the water and the ox-teams calling to each other on the towpath, she dies. It is very quiet under the awning.

branches.title: Stay with her
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stay beside her a while longer, with her hand in yours.

success.title: She is gone
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You sit with her until someone comes.

the-ford.title: The Ford
the-ford.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: It happens when the convoy is spread thinnest, with a dozen barges stuck in the middle of the ford and everyone in the water up to their knees.

First a rope goes slack. Then another, and another, all along the line, and the barges they were dragging start to slew round in the current. People are shouting, but not in a way you understand yet. Somebody on the far bank screams. There is smoke over there, suddenly, low and dark, from more than one place.

Then someone near you says, "Saints," very quietly, and points downstream.

Things are coming up out of the water. They stand up from the bottom of the ford where there was nothing a moment ago, one after another, with river weed hanging off them, and they start to walk toward the barges. There are dozens of them. They are coming the way people walk in a procession, all together, all the same way.

Everyone is running, or trying to. [who:regard-clerk] is standing up in the stern of his barge in the middle of the ford, with both arms round the manifest chest.

branches.title: Get on the rope and help drag the clerk's barge across
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Get your hands on the clerk's barge's rope with the passengers still pulling, and drag it the rest of the way to the far bank before the things in the water reach it.

success.title: The end of the rope
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You throw your weight on the rope and it comes toward you far too easily: the other end has come free. You haul it in, hand over hand, and look at the end. It is cut. Not frayed, not snapped: cut clean, as if with one stroke of a blade.

So you get your shoulder against the barge's side instead, with a dozen others, and heave, and it grinds over the gravel toward the bank. Over your shoulder you can see the dead coming across the ford in a long line, keeping step, as if someone were driving them. [who:regard-clerk] sees you in the water from the stern and shouts something you cannot hear.

The far bank is close now. You are soaked to the neck and frozen, and still alive.

failure.title: Dragged clear
failure.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You throw your weight on the rope and it comes toward you far too easily. You go over backwards into the water, and the current takes you, and you are rolling along the gravel under the surface toward the line of dead coming across the ford.

A hand gets you by the collar and hauls. It is [who:regard-clerk], out of his barge and up to his waist in the river, pulling you in against the hull. "Hold on to the barge," he shouts. "Hold on to it!" Then something under the water takes him by the leg, and he screams, and goes down, and comes up again, and keeps hold of you anyway.

You owe him your life. You are both hurt.

branches.title: Get to the escort captain and tell him to stop the barges behind
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Wade to where the escort captain sits his horse in the shallows, and make him stop the barges still waiting on the near bank.

success.title: He listens
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You grab his stirrup. "Stop them!" you shout. "Stop the ones behind! There's nothing to cross to!" He looks down at you, a hauler, mud to the eyes, and then he looks at the far bank, and you see him decide. "Hold the barges!" he roars. "Hold them on the near side!" The signal goes back down the line. The barges still waiting stay where they are. The ones already in the ford are on their own.

From beside his horse, higher than the water, you can see the far bank clearly, and it is not what you thought. There are fires along it, set in a line, and in the trees behind the fires there are men. Living men, standing still, watching.

failure.title: He ignores a hauler
failure.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You grab his stirrup and shout at him to stop the barges behind. He kicks your hand away. "Get back on your rope, hauler!" He turns his horse toward the far bank and spurs it on through the water.

Standing where his horse stood, you can see the far bank clearly, and it is not what you thought. There are fires along it, set in a line, and in the trees behind the fires there are men. Living men, standing still, watching. Someone else heard what you shouted: out in the ford, [who:regard-clerk] has his book open on the chest in the stern of his barge, and he is writing.

branches.title: Run for the far bank
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Let go of everything, and run for the far bank through the water as fast as you can.

success.title: You run
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You run. The water drags at your legs and the gravel rolls under your feet, and all around you other people are running too, and falling, and not getting up.

You see the dead coming across the ford beside you, close enough to touch: all in a line, all keeping pace, not one of them turning aside for anything, as if something were herding them. You do not stop. You reach the shallows by the far bank on your hands and knees, and crawl.

When you look back, [who:regard-clerk] is still out there in the middle of the ford, in the stern of his barge, holding on to the chest. He is looking straight at you.

branches.title: Get to the clerk's barge, and stay with him and the chest
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Wade out to the clerk's barge in the middle of the ford, climb aboard, and stand with him over the manifest chest.

success.title: Guarding the manifest's chest
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He is so surprised to see you that he laughs. "The manifest," he says. "If this goes in the river, nobody will ever know what we carried. Nobody will know who we were." So you stand over the chest together with a boat-hook and an oar.

From the stern you can see the far bank, where fires have been lit in a long line, and there are men moving in the trees behind them. Then the dead reach the barge. One of them gets a hand on your leg over the side and drags its nails through your boot. You beat it off. [who:regard-clerk] talks the whole time, without stopping, in a high fast voice: "Never this low. Never. The keeper at the waystation should have sent word. Why didn't he send word?"

the-gate-queue.title: The Gate Queue
the-gate-queue.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The queue for the land gate starts before dawn. The watch let the counted in first, with a nod. The half-counted wait until it suits them.

Today the queue is slower than ever. Inside, the streets are setting out feast tables for the convoy, which is days late, and you can smell the baking from here. A watchman walks the queue, looking at faces, and at hands.

branches.title: Slip in past the watch
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Wait for a big cart to go through, and slip in beside it on the side away from the watch.

success.title: A loaf, and a witness
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You walk in beside the cart's back wheel with your head down, and nobody stops you. Inside the walls the streets are full of tables and green branches and people too busy to look at you. You take a loaf off the end of a feast table as you pass and put it under your coat.

When you look up, a little girl in a clean dress is standing in a doorway, watching you. She saw. She looks at the loaf-shaped bulge under your coat, and then at your face, and she does not say anything. Not yet.

failure.title: Caught, and offered work
failure.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You are three steps past the gate when a hand closes on your collar. The watchman drags you back through, writes your name in his book, and shoves you into the mud of the road. "Half-counted and a sneak," he says. "I'll know you next time."

As you get up, a gate clerk in an inky coat comes over from his table. "I could use someone who moves quietly," he says in a low voice. "A day's work inside, paid in bread. All you'd have to do is bring me a name." He does not say whose name, or why. "Think about it," he says, and goes back to his table.

branches.title: Wait in the queue
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stand in the queue like everyone else, and wait your turn.

success.title: The gate closes early
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You wait all morning, shuffling forward a step at a time. The smell of the baking gets stronger. At noon, when you are ten people from the gate, a watchman walks down the queue shouting that the gate is closing early for the charter feast. "Come back tomorrow," he says. "Or don't."

The people ahead of you argue, and then give up. You walk back to your lean-to with nothing, and your stomach reminds you of it all the way.

the-halt.title: The Halt
the-halt.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The convoy halts for the night on a gravel bank a few hours short of the ford. There is no waystation, so there are no walls again. The haulers make their fires in a long line along the water.

Your crew's fire is quiet. There is a gap in the ring where [who:regard-partner] slept last night, and nobody fills it.

{if [q:prologue-first-death-river-burned] > 0}"You did right by him," says the oldest hauler, and passes you the pot. "The escort will have your name now. That's the price of it. It's always been the price of it." Later the sergeant comes along the fires asking which one of you lit a burning on the towpath. Nobody answers him, but everybody knows.{else}{if [q:prologue-partner-out-there] > 0}Nobody passes you the pot until you ask for it. "He was one of ours," the oldest hauler says at last, looking at the fire and not at you. "Now he's one of theirs, out there somewhere. We'll meet him again, likely, on some haul or other. I hope it's not me that does." Nobody else says anything at all.{else}"Sealed proper, with the words," says the oldest hauler, and passes you the pot. "His mother will like that, when she hears. More than a fire." He spits into the flames. "Cost you, though. I saw your face."{/if}{/if}

[who:regard-clerk] comes along the fires late, with his book and a lantern, to take the evening count. When he reaches your fire, he counts one fewer, and writes it down, and for once he says nothing about wages.

branches.title: Take up the rope in the morning
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Sleep, and take up the rope at first light for the last haul to the ford.

success.title: The ford ahead
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: At first light you take up the rope.

the-landing.title: The Landing
the-landing.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The harvest is in. The fields behind the village are stubble, and the last carts of grain have gone down the lane to the landing, where the barges wait in a line along the bank.

The old churchyard sits on the rise above the river. Your family's dead lie there, the way everyone's dead lie in the heartland: in the ground, under a stone, and they stay there. Nobody in the parish can say why the dead keep still here when they walk everywhere else. Nobody asks too loudly, in case asking changes it.

Below the churchyard, the landing is full. There are grain sacks stacked higher than a man, oxen being led onto the towpath, families saying goodbye, and a priest on the steps with a bowl of holy water. This is the convoy: the one haul of the year, upriver against the current, six weeks north to the frontier city. It is bigger this year than anyone remembers. People say it is a charter year, whatever that will mean for them.

You have a pack on your back and everything you own in it. You are leaving today.

branches.title: Go down to the landing
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take one last look at the churchyard, then go down the steps to the landing.

success.title: Down the steps
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You go down the steps to the landing.

the-late-barge-continues.title: The Late Barge Continues
the-late-barge-continues.intro: PLACEHOLDER: The Late Barge continues in a later build.

branches.title: Wait
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Wait, for now.

success.title: Time passes
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Time passes.

the-lean-to.title: The Lean-To
the-lean-to.intro: PLACEHOLDER: Your lean-to: three poles and a roof of boards and sacking, built against the outside of the city wall, where the stones keep off the worst of the wind. There is room to lie down and room to sit up, and a hole under the floor where you hide what matters. On the other side of the stones, a few feet away, people sleep in beds.{if [q:hunger] >= 3} There is not much in the hole under the floor, and you are hungry.{/if}{if [q:cold] >= 3} The cold comes straight through the sacking, and the wall is like ice at your back.{/if}

branches.title: Eat from your provisions
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take your food out of the hole under the floor, and eat it where nobody can see.

success.title: A meal
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: A hard end of bread, an apple going soft, a bit of cheese rind you have been saving. You eat it with your back to the opening so nobody passing can see what you have. It is not enough. It never is. But the hollow in your belly eases for a while.

branches.title: Lie down for the night
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Crawl in under the boards, pull the sacking across the opening, and sleep.

success.title: Night falls
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The night fires are burning again beyond the cleared strip, more of them than last night. The watch walks the district twice before midnight, and you hear them stop at the next lean-to, where the grandmother used to sleep. You lie still with your face to the wall until their boots go past, and at last, sleep comes.

the-long-haul.title: The Long Haul
the-long-haul.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The long haul: dawn to the noon halt without stopping, against a current that pulls like a live thing. Mid-morning, a length of tow-rope comes down the river past the line, turning slowly, the thick kind the convoy uses. Nobody stops.

At the front, the lead hauler is flagging. The barge-master pays extra for a good lead, and [who:regard-partner] is watching to see what you do.

branches.title: Take the lead rope
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go up the line and take the lead rope yourself, and set the pace for the whole line until the noon halt.

success.title: The barge-master notices
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You take the lead and you hold it. You find the rhythm and pull the line along with you, step after step, and the barge-master shouts from the deck that this is the best morning's haul since the heartland.

At the noon halt he comes down the plank and puts coins in your hand himself. "You'll lead again tomorrow," he says. "If you can still stand." You can barely stand. You are shaking with hunger, and your share of bread will not come close to filling you.

failure.title: The partner takes your weight
failure.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You take the lead, and for an hour you hold it. Then your legs start to go. The line slows behind you, the rope drags, and the barge-master starts shouting.

Suddenly the weight is less. [who:regard-partner] has come up behind you and taken half of it on his own shoulder, without being asked. "Lean on it," he says through his teeth. "I've got it. Just keep walking." He gets you both to the noon halt. You owe him, and you both know it.

branches.title: Pace yourself
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stay in your own place on the rope, and pace yourself for the whole day instead of the morning.

success.title: The clerk docks your wages
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You keep your own steady pace, and so does [who:regard-partner] beside you. The two of you talk in short breaths about nothing much: the weather, the river, his family on the lower bank.

At the noon halt the clerk comes down the line with his book. "Slow haul," he says, and docks you a penny each, as he said he would. [who:regard-partner] only shrugs. "Worth a penny," he says, "for the company."

the-low-ford.title: The Low Ford
the-low-ford.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The ford is a wide, shallow place where the river spreads out over gravel between two low wooded banks. In a normal year the barges float across it with a hand's breadth under their keels. This year the gravel is showing in long pale bars, and the water between them would not come up to your knees.

{if [q:origin]==2}You have hauled across this ford four times. You have never seen it like this. Nobody on your rope has.{else}Even you can see it is wrong. The crew are swearing, and the bargemaster is standing in the bow looking at the water as if it has insulted him.{/if}

The escort captain rides up and down the near bank, giving orders. "Lighten them! Everybody off who can walk. Passengers into the water, all of you, and put your backs into it. Haulers on both ropes. We drag them over one at a time and we don't stop till the last one's across." He stands in his stirrups and looks at the far bank, and the trees behind it. "And keep your eyes open."

So the convoy goes into the ford one barge at a time, dragged over the gravel by people up to their knees in cold water, and it strings out across the river for a mile: some barges across, some in the middle, most still waiting on the near bank. [who:regard-clerk]'s barge, with the manifest chest lashed down in the stern, is in the middle.

branches.title: Go down to the water
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go down into the cold water with everyone else.

success.title: Into the ford
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You go down into the water.

the-manifest-is-taken.title: The Manifest
the-manifest-is-taken.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: At the river gate, the council's men are waiting: a file of watchmen, and two men in the council's colours, one of them holding a paper with a seal on it. They walk straight past the wounded to the last barge.

"The convoy's manifest," the one with the paper says, "and all the convoy's papers. By order of the council."

{if [q:origin]<=2}[who:regard-clerk]{else}The clerk with the chest{/if} does not let go. "The manifest stays in my charge," he says, in a voice that shakes, "until the council's own clerk signs for it in the council's hall. That is the law of the convoy. It has been the law for thirty years."

"I am the council's clerk," the man says. "Consider it signed." Two watchmen take hold of the chest. The clerk holds on. They have to open his fingers one at a time. He is shouting now: "Count the wounded! Count the dead! There are people on the gravel back there! Nobody has counted them!"

{if [q:prologue-captain-fate]==2}The escort captain stands a few yards off with his arm strapped up, and watches, and says nothing.{/if} The council's men carry the chest in through the gate, and it shuts behind them. The crowd on the quay watched every moment of it. So did the priestess in grey.

branches.title: Look around at the gate
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stand on the quay among the survivors and the crowd, and decide where you are needed.

success.title: Taken
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You look around the quay.

the-night-fires.title: The Night Fires
the-night-fires.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: At dusk the city lights the night fires on the burning ground beyond the district: the dead nobody paid for, burned as a sentence. Tonight there are four pyres.

On the road below the wall, the family from the next lean-to are going out toward the glow, the grandmother wrapped in every blanket they own, coughing. "People go," the mother says when she sees you. "To see who it is."

branches.title: Watch the city burn the uncounted
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Walk out to the edge of the burning ground with the family, and watch the fires until they burn down.

success.title: Someone the lean-to knew
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You stand at the edge of the burning ground with the family and a few dozen others, in the smoke, while the watch leans on their spears and looks bored. On the second pyre, when the cloth burns away, the mother makes a small sound. She knew the face: a woman from the road they came in by.

"She was counted, where we came from," the mother whispers. "Here she's nothing." She holds the grandmother's arm very tight. "Not like that," she says. "Not for us. I won't let them." You stay until the pyres are embers and the cold has got right into your bones. Your coat is rolled up in your lean-to, and you never went back for it.

branches.title: Turn away
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Turn back. Go home to your lean-to, pull the sacking across, and try not to think about it.

success.title: A bad night's sleep
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You go back to your lean-to, pull the sacking over the opening, and lie with your face to the stones. It doesn't help. The smoke comes in anyway, and the smell with it: fat, and hair, and wet wood. Outside, you hear the family come back, and the mother crying, and the grandmother coughing and coughing.

You lie awake a long time, shaking, and the lean-to is cold. Your coat is rolled up beside you, and you never think to put it on.

the-notice-board.title: The Notice Board
the-notice-board.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The council has pinned a notice to the board in the square: what it expects the new charter to ask of the city. A crowd stands in front of it, mostly pretending to read.

[who:regard-neighbour] is near the front with her youngest on her hip. "Can you make it out?" she asks you. "I can never read the council's hand."

branches.title: Read the charter notice
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Push your way to the board, and read the notice yourself, line by line.

success.title: New quotas
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The council's clerk writes a tight, crabbed hand, but you get through it. Most of it is thanks to the king. The part that matters is near the bottom: new levy quotas, street by street, to send people north to the push. Your street is on the list. It owes six.

"What does it say?" [who:regard-neighbour] asks. You tell her. She hitches the child higher on her hip and looks at the doors along your street, counting, the way everyone around you has started to count.

failure.title: A stranger's reading
failure.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The council's clerk writes a tight, crabbed hand, and the longer you look, the less of it you can read. A man at your elbow offers to read it out for a penny. You pay him.

He reads it loud, for the whole crowd, and adds his own opinions as he goes. "Levy quotas, street by street. That's you lot sent north to feed the push, while the council sits warm." You are fairly sure some of it is not on the board at all. [who:regard-neighbour] looks frightened, and you cannot tell her which part was true.

branches.title: Ask your neighbour to read it
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask [who:regard-neighbour] to try reading it for you, and stand with her while she does.

success.title: A partial reading
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She reads it slowly, with her finger under the words and the child pulling at her hair. She gets about half of it. "Something about the levy," she says. "And streets. And something about the new roll. That's the part I care about." She tells you, shyly, that her husband's brother is on the new roll, and that when the charter comes, the whole family will be better placed. "It's all in that convoy," she says. "Everything we're waiting for."

You understand some of the notice. Not the part about the levy.

the-open-gate.title: The Open Gate
the-open-gate.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: Late in the day the barges reach the last waystation before the ford: stone walls on a rise, a tower at one corner. There should be lamps, and smoke, and a boy on the landing waving the barges in. There is nothing. The gate hangs open on one hinge, and crows walk on the wall.

"I want eight with me," the escort captain calls across the water. "Passengers too, if you've the stomach." Nobody answers at first.

branches.title: Go ashore with the escort
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Put your hand up. Go ashore with the captain and his men, and see for yourself.

success.title: The fallen waystation
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The yard inside the gate is empty. There is old blood on the stones, brown and flaking, and a cart turned on its side. Nothing moves. In the keeper's room his register lies open on the table, the ink dry. The last entry is dated days before the convoy was due.

"Nobody here," the captain says, too loudly. "Back to the boats."

By the time you are back aboard it is dark, and the wind off the water goes straight through your clothes. You are cold to the bone. Your coat is still rolled up in your pack.

success.title: Something moving
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You get as far as the gate. Then, somewhere in the dark yard, something moves: a scrape, and a sound like breathing. The escort stop dead.

"Back," the captain says quietly. "Walk. Don't run." You walk backwards to the boats with your heart hammering, and you never see what it was.

By the time you are back aboard it is dark, and you are cold and shaking. Your coat is still rolled up in your pack.

branches.title: Stay aboard
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Keep your hands down. Stay aboard, and let the escort look.

success.title: Two stories
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The captain and his men are gone a long time. When they come back he tells the barges that the keeper must have abandoned the place, "packed up and gone, it happens." Nobody on your barge believes him. The crew whisper to each other that the dead took it, that they saw blood on the stones.

With no walls to shelter behind, the barges tie up in midstream for the night. The cold comes off the water. Your coat is still rolled up in your pack.

the-reeds.title: The Reeds
the-reeds.intro: PLACEHOLDER: The survivors' camp on the far bank of the ford: a long, ragged line of people among the reeds, with the barges that crossed tied up along the shore and the escort's pickets facing the trees. Your barge's hold is somewhere under the water, or on its side on a gravel bar. What you carried out of the ford is all you have.{if [q:hunger] >= 3} You have not eaten since the morning.{/if}{if [q:cold] >= 3} Your clothes are still wet, and the cold has got into your bones.{/if}

branches.title: Eat what you carried out of the water
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Sit down in the reeds and eat what you managed to carry out of the water.

success.title: Wet bread
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The bread in your pack is soaked through and gritty with river sand. You eat it anyway, slowly, and it is the best thing you have ever tasted. Somebody passes you a cup of something hot without a word, and you pass it on.

branches.title: Lie down among the reeds
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Find a flat place among the reeds, near a fire, and lie down for the night.

success.title: Night on the far bank
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You lie down in the reeds with your back to a fire and your face to the dark. Nobody around you is really asleep. Every time the water splashes out in the ford, the whole camp goes quiet and listens.

the-rider.title: The Rider
the-rider.intro:
{if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: The rider is sliding out of the saddle as the watch get to him. They catch him and lower him to the cobbles, and the crowd surges forward to hear. He is trying to say something. His lips are moving, and he keeps lifting one hand and pointing back the way he came, downriver.

Then the council's men arrive: four of them, in the council's colours, pushing through the crowd with their elbows. "Stand back! Council business! Stand back there!" They are going to carry him off before anyone hears a word, and you are still six rows back.{else}PLACEHOLDER: You get to him first. He is lying on his side in the road with his hand pressed to his ribs, and the blood is coming through his fingers. He is younger than you thought. When he sees you he grabs your coat.

"The ford," he says. "They're at the ford. Waiting. Men in the trees on this side, dozens of them, and fires laid ready, not lit. And the dead." He pulls you closer. "The dead are with them. On the river road. Walking along with them like cattle going to market, and the men not even afraid of them. They didn't touch the men. They came for us." He coughs, and it is red. "They got the others. The convoy's walking into it. Somebody has to tell them."

Boots are coming down the road from the gate: the watch, at a run. You are the only one who heard.{/if}

branches.title: Tell the priestess what he said
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: When the watch have taken him, go and find the death-watch priestess, who is working among the lean-tos today, and tell her everything he said.

success.title: She listens
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The watch drag you off him and carry him away toward the gate. A watchman takes a long look at your face before he goes.

You find the priestess in grey kneeling in a lean-to three rows over, with her nail-bag open, and you tell her all of it. She listens without interrupting, and her face gets very still. "[who:regard-priestess]," she says at the end, as if giving you her name is part of the answer. "Thank you. I'll take it to the people who ought to hear it." She looks up at the wall. "Whether they want to is another thing."

branches.title: Keep it to yourself
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Say nothing to anyone. Let the watch take him, and keep what he told you to yourself.

success.title: Only you know
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The watch drag you off him and carry him away toward the gate, and he is still trying to talk. A watchman takes a long look at your face before he goes. "What did he say to you?" he asks. "Nothing," you say. "He was raving." The watchman writes something down anyway.

Only you know. Men at the ford, waiting. The dead walking with them. You go back to your lean-to and sit with it, and it does not get any lighter.

branches.title: Push to the front
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Push, shove and elbow your way to the front of the crowd before the council's men get to him.

success.title: A few words
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You get to the front just as the council's men reach him, close enough to hear. His voice is a thread. "The dead on the river road," he is saying, over and over. "The dead on the river road. And men with them. Men with them." Then the council's men have him up by the arms and legs and are carrying him away through the crowd.

One of them, the last, looks back at the crowd, and looks straight at you, and at the people around you who heard. He does not look pleased.

failure.title: Shoved back
failure.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The crowd is too thick, and a big man with a basket plants his elbow in your chest and shoves you back. By the time you get your breath, the council's men are carrying the rider off.

You climb up on a mounting block to see where they take him. They do not take him to the hospital, or to the church, or to the council hall. They carry him up the hill and in through the side door of a big private house with a painted door, and the door shuts. You know whose house it is. Everyone in the city knows whose house it is.

branches.title: Stay back
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stay where you are at the back of the crowd, and watch what happens.

success.title: Carried off
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You stay where you are. From the back of the crowd you see the council's men lift him and carry him off at a half-run, with a cloak over his face. Nobody hears anything he says, if he says anything at all.

All you know is what you saw: six riders went downriver to look for the convoy, and one came back, alone, like that.

the-road-to-the-gate.title: The Survivors
the-road-to-the-gate.intro:
{if [q:origin]<=2}PLACEHOLDER: The last day's haul is the longest of the six weeks. The survivors drag the barges that crossed up the last stretch of river with half the haulers they need, and the ones who can't haul walk alongside, carrying the ones who can't walk.

Then the river bends, and there it is: the city, on its hill at the foot of the rapids, with its walls and towers and the smoke of its chimneys going up. The river gate is open. There is a crowd on the quay, hundreds of people, waiting. As the first barge comes in, the crowd goes silent, counting the barges, and then counting them again.

[who:regard-clerk] rides on the last barge, lying on a door with his leg bound up, with both arms round the manifest chest. At the river gate, a woman in grey with a leather bag across her body is waiting for the wounded.{else}PLACEHOLDER: The news comes up from the river gate at noon: barges. Everyone in the city who can walk goes down to the quay. You go with them.

The crowd is hundreds deep by the time the first barge comes round the bend below the rapids, and it goes quiet to count them. There are not many. Then there are no more. The barges are low in the water, and the people walking beside them on the towpath are muddy and bloody and silent. Some are being carried.

On the last barge, a thin man in a black coat is lying on a door with his leg bound up, holding an iron-bound chest in both arms as if it were a child. {if [q:met-priestess] > 0}[who:regard-priestess] is waiting at the river gate with her nail-bag, for the wounded and the dead.{else}At the river gate, the death-watch priestess is waiting with her nail-bag, for the wounded and the dead.{/if}{/if}

branches.title: Go on to the gate
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go on to the river gate with everyone else.

success.title: The gate
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You go on to the gate.

the-rope.title: The Rope
the-rope.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: Grey morning on the towpath, a few days short of the ford, and the river is lower than it should be. The haulers stand forty to a rope, stamping and blowing on their hands.

The convoy's tally-clerk walks the line with his book: a thin man in the only clean black coat on the towpath. He counts every hauler onto the rope by name, and anyone slow loses a day's wage. "Every day we're late," he says, "the ford drops another finger."

The hauler taking the rope beside you is new to your crew: a young man with big raw hands, who has not said a word yet. Something happens while the clerk works his way toward you.

branches.title: Devout
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Say the haulers' prayer for the rope out loud before you take it up, all of it, though the clerk is standing there waiting.

success.title: Amen on the towpath
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The clerk waits, pen lifted, until you finish, and then says "Amen" with you, which you did not expect. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk," he says. "It does no harm to ask." He counts you onto the rope with no mark against you.

The young man beside you finished the prayer with you under his breath. "My mother made me learn it," he says, as the rope comes taut. "[who:regard-partner]. Let's hope somebody's listening."

branches.title: Doubter
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The clerk tells the line that the chaplain blessed this haul at dawn. Say, loud enough to carry, that the chaplain rides the barge and the haulers pull it.

success.title: The chaplain rides
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: Half the line laughs. The young man beside you laughs loudest, then catches the clerk's eye and stops.

"[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk," the clerk says to you, very evenly. "I'll tell the chaplain you said so. He'll be delighted." He counts you onto the rope and looks at you a moment longer than at the others.

"[who:regard-partner]," the young man says out of the side of his mouth. "You'll get us both docked. I like you."

branches.title: Soft-hearted
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The old hauler at the end of the line is slow because of his bad knee, and the clerk is heading for him with his pen. Step out and ask the clerk not to dock him.

success.title: Not today
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The clerk stops and looks at the old man's knee, which is swollen through his trousers. "One day," he says at last. "Not two." He turns to you. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. I'll remember who asked."

The young man beside you watched the whole thing. "[who:regard-partner]," he says. "I'll pull the old man's share on the hills. Between us we'll get him to the city."

branches.title: Hard-hearted
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The clerk asks the line who was slowest on the rope yesterday. Point at the old hauler with the bad knee.

success.title: Docked
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The clerk writes it down and docks the old man a day's wage. The old man says nothing at all, which is worse than if he had cursed you. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk," the clerk tells you. "Thank you for your honesty."

The young man beside you does not speak for most of the morning. When he does, it is only because the rope is long and the day is longer. "[who:regard-partner]," he says. "Just so you know who's next to you."

branches.title: Proud
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The clerk marks you down as slow for coming last to the rope. Tell him to his face that you pulled more than any hauler on this line yesterday, and he knows it.

success.title: A second mark
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He hears you out, and does not take the mark away. He makes a second mark beside it. "For the speech," he says. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. I know exactly what everyone pulled yesterday. It's my job."

The young man beside you whistles low. "[who:regard-partner]," he says. "Remind me never to argue with you. Or with him."

branches.title: Grasping
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask the clerk to read out what you are owed so far this haul, and check his figures against the count you have been keeping in your head.

success.title: Right to the penny
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He reads it out, day by day, and makes you listen to every line. His count is right to the penny. So is yours. He almost smiles. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. Most haulers can't count past their fingers."

The young man beside you asks what you are owed, and whistles at the answer. "[who:regard-partner]. I'm owed less than that, and I've pulled just as hard. Maybe I should start counting too."

branches.title: Curious
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Ask the clerk what rides under the canvas on the last barge, the one with two of the escort sitting beside it day and night.

success.title: Under the canvas
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He tells you, which surprises you. "Powder and shot for the garrisons. Nails for the Seal. And the charter." He sees your face. "The new king's charter for the frontier, and everything that comes with it. Now haul." He writes you down. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. You ask a lot of questions for a hauler."

The young man beside you heard it all. "[who:regard-partner]," he says. "A king's charter. On our rope. Pull careful, then."

branches.title: Loyal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A barge-master on the next rope calls for haulers to come over to his line, at a better wage. Stay on the rope you signed on for.

success.title: Signed for this one
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: Half the line goes, and your rope is short-handed all morning. The clerk sees who stayed, and makes a note in your favour. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. The ones who stay are the ones I remember at the pay table."

The young man beside you stayed too. "[who:regard-partner]," he says. "My father said a hauler who changes ropes for money changes them for anything."

branches.title: Hot-tempered
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The clerk docks the hauler in front of you a day's wage for one stumble on the wet bank. Knock the tally-stick out of his hand.

success.title: The tally-stick in the mud
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The stick goes into the mud. The whole line goes quiet. The clerk looks at the stick for a moment, then picks it up, wipes it on his coat, and writes your name in his book. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk," he says. "Now I'll know you anywhere."

The young man beside you pulls you back onto the rope before the escort can ride over. "[who:regard-partner]," he says. "Keep your hands on the rope, you fool. Both of them."

branches.title: Teetotal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The barge-master's morning jug of spirits comes down the line to warm the haulers. Pass it on without drinking.

success.title: A clear head on the rope
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The young man beside you drinks your share, and grins, and wipes his mouth. "[who:regard-partner]. I'll pull your share too, then, while it lasts."

The clerk notices, as he notices everything. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk," he says, counting you onto the rope. "The only sober hauler on the river. I'll put you at the front if we reach a hard stretch."

branches.title: Hearty appetite
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Eat your whole day's bread ration now, before the rope moves, while the clerk is still counting down the line.

success.title: Bread before the rope
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: It is gone before the clerk reaches you. He looks at the crumbs on your shirt. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk. That was meant to last till dark."

The young man beside you laughs. "You'll be eating the rope by noon," he says. "[who:regard-partner]." Later, at the noon halt, he gives you a crust he kept back from his own share, and says nothing about it.

branches.title: Grave-shy
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: There is a charred post on the towpath where the haulers burned one of their own last year. Step off the path to go around it, though it puts you last on the rope.

success.title: Last on the rope
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The clerk marks you last. "[who:regard-clerk], tally-clerk," he says. "It's a post. It can't hurt you."

The young man beside you went around it too, you notice, and caught up just behind you. "[who:regard-partner]," he says. "We burned my uncle at a post like that. I don't walk past them either."

the-rope-partner-dies.title: On the Towpath
the-rope-partner-dies.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: The line is already moving again, and the haulers are looking at you, because you were his partner on the rope. Whatever happens to him is yours to decide.

On the river everybody knows what the dead do if you leave them. Haulers have their own way: a fire on the bank, quick and hot, and the ashes into the river. It works. It is also against the law and the church, and the escort are riding up and down the line.

The proper way is the Seal. The clerk carries nails, and the convoy stops at the next halt in three hours. But three hours is a long time to carry a body on a barge full of people, and sometimes they do not wait that long.

The third way is to leave him where he lies, and keep your place on the rope.

branches.title: Burn the body, as haulers do
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Drop out of the line and build a fire on the bank from driftwood, and burn him now, the haulers' way.

success.title: A burning outside the rite
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: Two of the older haulers drop out to help you without a word. You drag driftwood down from the tide line and build it high, and put him on it, and light it. It burns hot. He will not rise.

You are still standing in the smoke when an escort rider comes back down the towpath at a trot. He stops and looks at the fire, and at what is in it, for a long time. Then he takes out a little book and writes something, and asks your name. You give it. He rides on without a word.

branches.title: Carry it on for the Seal
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Carry him down the bank to the barge, and lay him on the deck under sacking until the halt, where the clerk can seal him properly.

success.title: Sealed at the halt
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The bargemen don't like it, but they let you lay him on the deck under sacking, and you walk the rest of the haul beside the barge, watching. Nothing happens. At the halt [who:regard-clerk] comes down the bank with his bag, and seals him in front of the whole crew, with the prayers said properly, all of them.

"Thank you for bringing him," the clerk says afterwards, entering the nail in his book. "Most haulers wouldn't have bothered. They'd have burned him in a ditch." He writes the name carefully, the whole name.

success.title: It moves under the sacking
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The bargemen don't like it, but they let you lay him on the deck under sacking, and you walk the rest of the haul beside the barge, watching.

An hour short of the halt, one of the bargemen shouts. The sacking is moving.

branches.title: Leave it
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Leave him where he lies, and go back to your place on the rope before the line gets too far ahead.

success.title: Kept up with the convoy
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: You take your place on the rope. For the rest of the haul you do not look back, but other people do. You hear them talking in low voices behind you, and you hear your name.

By the time the convoy reaches the halt, the towpath behind you is empty for a mile. Somewhere back there, he is lying on the clay. Tonight or tomorrow, he will get up.

the-row-afterwards.title: The Row Afterwards

branches.title: Go out to the road
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go out to the road below the wall to see who is coming.

success.title: The road
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You go out to the road.

the-street-afterwards.title: The Street Afterwards
the-street-afterwards.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: By noon the whole street knows. Neighbours who never spoke to [who:regard-neighbour] in her life stand in their doorways talking about her in low voices. The feast branches are still hanging over her door.

{if [q:prologue-first-death-city-paid] > 0}People nod to you as you pass, and one old woman stops you to press your hand. "That was a godly thing you did," she says. "Most wouldn't." Her son, beside her, is looking at your purse. By the afternoon everyone in the street knows that you had the money for a stranger's Seal, and you have the feeling some of them are working out how much more you might have.{else}{if [q:prologue-first-death-city-burned] > 0}The street is quieter around you than it was yesterday. Nobody says anything to your face. But the woman across the way pulls her children indoors when you come out, and the baker gives you the burnt loaf without meeting your eye. Next door the shutters stay closed all day. Behind them, the children are crying.{else}"She seals half the poor in this quarter out of her own purse," the baker tells you, when you mention the priestess. "Everyone knows. Nobody says. The church would stop her if it knew." He gives you your bread. "You drove a hard bargain for them. Good. Somebody should."{/if}{/if}

The priestess walks back down the street toward the gate with her bag, and the people in the doorways step back to let her pass. She is already late for the next house.

In the afternoon, a shout goes up from the direction of the gate, and then another, and people start to run.

branches.title: Follow the crowd to the gate
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Follow the running people down toward the gate.

success.title: The rest of the day
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You follow them down toward the gate.

the-survivors.title: On the Quay

branches.title: Stay with the tally-clerk
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Sit down on the quay beside [who:regard-clerk], and stay with him.

success.title: Nothing to count
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He does not look at you for a long time. "Six weeks," he says at last. "Every sack. Every name. And they didn't even count the wounded." He looks at the shut gate. "They wanted the book. Only the book. Why would you want the book, and not the people?"

The priestess in grey comes past with a bucket and stops to look at his leg. "[who:regard-priestess]," she tells you, when you ask. "Keep him still. I'll come back when I can." She does not come back for a long time.

{if [q:origin]==1}The watch come down the quay with their book. You are a heartlander, off the convoy: not on the city's count. They write you down as uncounted.{else}The watch come down the quay with their book. Haulers have never been on the city's count. They write you down as uncounted.{/if} By evening, the whole city knows the convoy is lost.

branches.title: Help the priestess in grey with the wounded
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go to the woman in grey, and help her with the wounded.

success.title: How the city handles its dead
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: She gives you a bucket and a pile of rags without asking who you are. "[who:regard-priestess]," she says, when she finally has a moment. "Death-watch. Hold this. Don't let go of it." You hold a man's arm while she stitches it.

She shows you how the city handles its dead: every death reported and written in the register, every body sealed or burned before dark, and no exceptions for anyone. "Especially not today," she says, looking back at the barges.

{if [q:origin]==1}The watch come down the quay with their book. You are a heartlander, off the convoy: not on the city's count. They write you down as uncounted.{else}The watch come down the quay with their book. Haulers have never been on the city's count. They write you down as uncounted.{/if} By evening, the whole city knows the convoy is lost.

branches.title: Go to the clerk who lost the chest
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Push through the crowd to the clerk sitting alone on the quay, and ask him what that chest was.

success.title: The convoy's tally-clerk
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: He looks up at you as if nobody has spoken to him in a week. "The convoy's manifest," he says. "Every sack, every keg, every name, every soul we carried. Everything the charter promised, and who to. Six weeks of it." He holds out an inky hand. "[who:regard-clerk]. Tally-clerk to the convoy. Or I was."

He tells you about the ford, in pieces, not in order: the ropes, the fires on the bank, the dead coming up out of the water. "And they took the book," he says. "Not the wounded. The book." By evening, the whole city knows the convoy is lost.

branches.title: Help the death-watch priestess carry in the wounded
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go to the priestess at the gate, and help her carry the wounded in from the barges.

success.title: The wounded
success.description:
{if [q:origin]==3 || [q:prologue-first-death-outside-priestess]==1 || [q:prologue-passed-on-the-rider]==1}PLACEHOLDER: She sees you coming and hands you the end of a stretcher without a word. "Good," she says. "You again. Lift."{else}PLACEHOLDER: She hands you the end of a stretcher before you have finished offering. "[who:regard-priestess]," she says. "Death-watch. Lift on three."{/if} You carry the wounded in through the gate all afternoon.

The clerk who lost the chest helps, on a crutch, holding lanterns and doors. "[who:regard-clerk]," he tells you, when you ask. "The convoy's tally-clerk. I have nothing left to count, so I might as well carry." By evening, the whole city knows the convoy is lost.

the-survivors-camp.title: The Survivors' Camp
the-survivors-camp.intro: {if [q:presence-clerk]==1}PLACEHOLDER: The survivors of the ford are camped on the quay outside the river gate, under sailcloth stretched between the empty barges. The city will not let them in until they have been counted, and nobody has come to count them. [who:regard-clerk] sits among them on a coil of rope, with his bad leg stretched out and a crutch beside him, and no chest. People still come to him with questions, out of habit. He still answers them.{else}PLACEHOLDER: The survivors of the ford are camped on the quay outside the river gate, under sailcloth stretched between the empty barges. [who:regard-clerk]'s place on the coil of rope is empty. Someone says he has gone to the gate again, to ask for his book back.{/if}

branches.title: Talk to the tally-clerk
branches.description: {if [q:presence-clerk]==1}PLACEHOLDER: Sit down on the quay beside him, and talk.{else}PLACEHOLDER: He isn't here. He has gone to the gate again, to ask for his book back.{/if}

success.title: A word with the clerk
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You sit down on the quay beside him.

the-tally-barge.title: The Tally Barge
the-tally-barge.intro: {if [q:presence-clerk]==3}PLACEHOLDER: The tally barge is moored at the edge of the survivors' camp. Under the awning at the stern, [who:regard-clerk] lies on a pallet with his leg bound up in bloody linen and the manifest chest beside him. He is grey and sweating, and he does not know anyone. An escort soldier sits on the chest with a musket across his knees, and turns away everyone who comes near.{else}PLACEHOLDER: The tally barge is the smallest in the convoy and the best kept. At the stern, under a canvas awning, [who:regard-clerk] sits at a folding table with the manifest open in front of him and the iron-bound manifest chest at his feet. Anyone with business about the count, or wages, or cargo, comes here. He looks up when you come aboard, and puts his pen down.{/if}

branches.title: Talk to the tally-clerk
branches.description: {if [q:presence-clerk]==3}PLACEHOLDER: He can't talk. He is lying under the awning with a fever from his wound, and the soldier on the chest won't let you near him.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Sit down on the upturned bucket across the table from him, and ask him about something.{/if}

success.title: A word with the clerk
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You sit down across the table from him.

the-towpath-camp.title: The Towpath Camp
the-towpath-camp.intro: PLACEHOLDER: Wherever the convoy stops, your crew makes camp in the same way: a fire on the bank below the towpath, the ropes coiled beside it, and forty haulers sleeping in a ring with their boots toward the flames. It is not much, but it is yours, and everyone in the ring knows your name.{if [q:hunger] >= 3} The smell of someone else's supper is hard to bear.{/if}{if [q:cold] >= 3} Even close to the fire, the cold off the river gets into your bones.{/if}

branches.title: Eat from your provisions
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Sit by the fire and eat from the rations in your pack.

success.title: A meal
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: A heel of bread, a strip of dried fish, and water from the river boiled with a handful of oats. You eat it hot off the fire with your fingers. It is gone too quickly, but the gnawing in your belly goes quiet.

branches.title: Lie down for the night
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Lie down in the ring with your boots to the fire, and try to sleep.

success.title: Night falls
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The ring is smaller tonight. Nobody says so. The escort has put pickets all round the camp, and every time a log shifts on the fire someone sits up with a knife in his hand. You lie with your back to the flames and your face to the dark, and listen to the river, until at last you sleep.

the-watch-sees-the-smoke.title: The Watch Comes
the-watch-sees-the-smoke.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: They come round the end of the wall at a run: four watchmen and the sergeant from the search, with cudgels out. The fire is too big to put out now, and they know it. The sergeant stops at the edge of the ditch and looks at what is burning.

"Whose fire is this?" he says. Nobody answers. The father has his arms round his children. The mother is staring at the sergeant as if she would like to put him on the fire too.

"I asked a question," the sergeant says. "Somebody built this. Somebody's going in the book for it. I'd rather it was the right somebody."

There is still time to step back between the lean-tos and be somewhere else.

branches.title: Stand with the family at the fire
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stay where you are beside the father, and tell the sergeant you helped build it.

success.title: Your name in the book
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: The sergeant looks at you for a long moment. "You again," he says. He writes your name in his book, slowly, so you can see him do it. Then he writes the father's. "Burning outside the rite. The magistrate will hear of it." The watch kick the edges of the fire in, but it has done its work.

When they have gone, the mother comes and takes your face in her cold hands and kisses your forehead, like a blessing. "You stood with us," she says. "We won't forget it. Not ever."

branches.title: Slip away before they get here
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Step back into the gap between two lean-tos, and walk away before the sergeant looks in your direction.

success.title: Gone before they came
success.description:
PLACEHOLDER: Nobody stops you. You walk away down the row with your heart pounding, and you do not look back until you are behind your own sacking.

From there you hear the sergeant shouting, and the father answering, and then a blow, and a child screaming. The watch take the father to the gate. He comes back hours later with his face swollen and his name in the magistrate's book, alone. The fire burned down on its own. Nobody in the family says anything to you about where you were.

what-is-lost.title: What Is Lost
what-is-lost.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: By nightfall the city knows. Not from the council, which has said nothing, but from the survivors on the quay, from the watch, from the barge crews in the taverns by the river gate. The convoy is lost at the ford. Eighty barges out of a hundred, the survivors say. The grain for the winter. The nails and the powder. And the charter chest, with everything the new king promised the frontier: the new roll of citizens, the land grants, the appointments to the new offices. All of it is lying in the ford, or burned, or in somebody's hands.

People stand in the streets in the dark and talk about what they were waiting for. A place on the count. A patch of ground. An office. A husband, a sister, a son coming upriver.

{if [q:prologue-clerk-told-charter] > 0}You remember [who:regard-clerk] at his table on the tally barge, counting the chest's contents off on his inky fingers. "Names. The chest is full of names." {/if}{if [q:origin]==1}{if [q:prologue-left-because-sent-for] > 0}The letter that sent for you is still in your pack. It promised you something that was coming north in that chest.{else}You came six weeks up the river for a new life. You had not thought, until tonight, how much of it was coming north in somebody else's chest.{/if}{else}{if [q:origin]==2}Five weeks on the rope, and everything the convoy carried went through your hands: every sack, every keg, and the chest the escort guarded day and night. You hauled it all this way to watch it go into the river.{else}{if [q:origin]==3}{if [q:prologue-lead-levy-quota] > 0}You think of the notice in the square, and the people your street owes to the levy, and what the charter was supposed to give back in return.{else}You think of the feast tables, set and cleared and set again for a convoy that was never coming.{/if}{else}From outside the walls, you have watched the city wait for this convoy all month. You thought it had nothing to do with you. It had everything to do with you.{/if}{/if}{/if}{if [q:bond] >= 1 && [q:bond] <= 16} And you think of the one you are tied to, and where they are tonight, and what this means for them.{/if}{if [q:keepsake-register-page] > 0} In your pack, the page from the register, with its one name struck out, feels heavier than paper should.{/if}

Something on that convoy was yours. You know exactly what it was.

branches.title: Think about what it means for you
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Stop pretending you don't know what you were waiting for.

success.title: Yours
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You know what it was.

what-people-see.title: What People See
what-people-see.intro: PLACEHOLDER: A stranger looks at you for a moment in the street, and makes up their mind. What do they see first? What will a witness remember about you, afterwards? Pick one thing, or two{if [q:features-picked] >= 1}. You have picked one already; pick another, or move on{/if}.

branches.title: Tall
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Tall: a head taller than most people in any crowd.

success.title: Tall
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: A head taller than most. People step aside for you without thinking, and listen when you speak, and remember you afterwards. You can see over any crowd. You cannot hide in one.

branches.title: Slight
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Slight: small, and lightly built.

success.title: Slight
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Small and light. People overlook you, underestimate you, and forget you were in the room, which has its uses. You fit through gaps other people can't. Nobody picks you for heavy work, and you are not as strong as you would like.

branches.title: Broad and heavy
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Broad and heavy: built like a barrel, with shoulders to match.

success.title: Broad and heavy
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Built for work. Work gangs want you, and people in a quarrel think twice before they start one with you. You are stronger than most. You also eat like two people, and hunger finds you faster than it finds anyone else.

branches.title: Pox-scarred
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Pox-scarred: a face pitted all over with old scars from the pox.

success.title: Pox-scarred
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You had the pox, and lived, and your face shows it for anyone to see. In a city that is terrified of plague, some people think that makes you safe to be near, since you can't catch it twice. Others think you carry it. Either way, they notice.

branches.title: Striking
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Striking: a face people turn round in the street to look at again.

success.title: Striking
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: People look at you, and keep looking. Doors open that would stay shut for other people, and people listen to you a little longer than they need to. The rich like you near them. The jealous remember you. Not all of the attention is the kind you want.

branches.title: Forgettable face
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A forgettable face: the kind nobody can describe an hour later.

success.title: Forgettable face
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Nobody remembers your face. People you met yesterday introduce themselves again. Witnesses to anything you do will argue about what you looked like, and word of what you did will travel slowly, because nobody can say who did it.

branches.title: Maimed hand
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A maimed hand: two fingers gone from one hand, long healed.

success.title: Maimed hand
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: A rope or a blade took the fingers, years ago. You have learned to manage, mostly, but fine work is harder, and a blade never sits quite right in that hand. Beggars and old soldiers look at your hand and take you for one of their own.

branches.title: Grey too young
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Grey too young: your hair went grey long before its time.

success.title: Grey too young
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Your hair went grey years before it should have. People look at it and assume you have seen something terrible, and they are not wrong. Old people talk to you as if you were one of them, and tell you things they would not tell the young.

branches.title: Soft hands
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Soft hands: hands that have plainly never done a day's hard labour.

success.title: Soft hands
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Your hands give you away. Anyone who shakes one knows at once you have never hauled a rope or dug a field. It marks you as better off, or as a heartlander, or both. Labourers do not trust you. Clerks and merchants take you for one of theirs.

branches.title: A limp
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A limp: one leg that drags a little with every step.

success.title: A limp
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: One leg drags a little, every step, and it always will. You are slower on the road than other people, and much slower if you have to run. Some people pity you for it. Some people pick on you for it. You have learned to tell them apart from a long way off.

branches.title: That's enough
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: That is enough. That is what strangers see.

success.title: Move on
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: That is how strangers will see you, and remember you, for the rest of your life. Now for where that life has been.

what-the-council-does.title: What the Council Says

branches.title: Go home
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Go home, before the watch start clearing the road.

success.title: Dusk
success.description: {if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: You go home through the emptying streets.{else}PLACEHOLDER: You go back along the wall to your lean-to before the watch clear the road.{/if}

what-was-aboard.title: What Was Aboard
what-was-aboard.intro: PLACEHOLDER: Late at night, you sit with it. The city is dark around you, except for the lamps at the gate and the glow of the night fires outside the walls. What were you waiting for, on that convoy? What did the ford take from you?

branches.title: Belong
branches.description: {if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: A name on the new roll: not yours, you are already counted, but someone in your house who is not, and was going to be.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Your name on the new roll of citizens. A place on the count, with everything it brings: bread when bread is short, a rite when you die, and a door with your number painted on it.{/if}

success.title: Belong
success.description: {if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: The roll is at the bottom of the ford, or in the council's hands. Without it, the one you were waiting for stays what they were yesterday: uncounted, fed last, burned if they die. The count decides who eats, and who goes to the fires. You mean to get them on it, charter or no charter.{else}PLACEHOLDER: The roll is at the bottom of the ford, or in the council's hands. Without it, you are what you were yesterday: {if [q:origin]==4}half-counted, fed last, and burned on the night fires if you die.{else}uncounted, fed last, and burned on the night fires if you die.{/if} The count decides who eats, and who goes to the fires. You mean to get on it, charter or no charter.{/if}

branches.title: Free ground
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A land grant beyond the walls, with your name on it: a piece of the frontier to clear and farm and hold, and nobody's leave needed to live on it.

success.title: Free ground
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The grant is gone with the convoy, the paper and the seal and the promise. But the land is still out there, beyond the cleared strip, where the free people burn their dead and the push has not reached yet. Nobody else is going to give it to you now. {if [q:trait]==9 || [q:trait]==5}You never liked asking anyway.{else}You mean to have it anyway.{/if}

branches.title: Rise
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: An appointment to one of the new offices the charter created, with your name written into it: a place in the crown's service, or the church's, and a door that would have opened.

success.title: Rise
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The appointment is gone with the convoy, and somebody else will fill the office if you don't. Somebody who was never promised it, and knows the right people. {if [q:trait]==6}You know what an office like that is worth, to the coin.{else}You have seen how this city works now.{/if} You mean to rise anyway, over the ones who are already climbing.

branches.title: Put them to rest
branches.description: {if [q:bond] == 9}PLACEHOLDER: Your betrothed, whom you have never met, coming upriver to marry you on one of the barges that never came in.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Someone you lost was on the convoy, travelling upriver, and did not come off the barges at the quay.{/if}

success.title: Put them to rest
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: They died at the ford. Nobody has sealed them, and nobody has burned them. They are lying out there in the water or on the gravel, unrited, and every one of the dead at that ford will get up. Maybe they already have. {if [q:trait]==12}The thought of going near them makes your skin crawl. You mean to go anyway.{else}Somebody has to go and put them to rest. It is going to be you.{/if}

what-you-carry.title: What You Carry
what-you-carry.intro: {if [q:origin]==1}PLACEHOLDER: That night, below deck, with the barge knocking against its mooring and the passengers snoring around you on the sacks, you open your pack by the light of the lamp at the ladder. Under your spare shirt, wrapped in a stocking, is the one thing you brought from before, from home. You take it out and hold it for a while.{else}{if [q:origin]==2}PLACEHOLDER: At the noon halt, with your shoulder raw from the rope, you sit on the towpath a little apart from the others and open your pack. At the bottom, where you always keep it, is the one thing you carry from before. You take it out and hold it for a while.{else}{if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: Home from the square, you bar the door, kneel by the hearth and lift the loose board beside it. Underneath, wrapped in a cloth, is the one thing you keep from before. Nobody else knows it is there. You take it out and hold it for a while.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Back at the lean-to, you check that nobody is watching, and dig with your fingers in the hole under the floor. It is still there, wrapped in oilcloth: the one thing you keep from before. You take it out and hold it for a while.{/if}{/if}{/if}

branches.title: A parent's knife
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Your mother's or your father's knife, with a notch cut in the handle for every risen it put down. Run your thumb down the notches, and count them.

success.title: Eleven notches
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Eleven notches. Eleven of the dead your parent put down with this blade, one at a time, up close. "It's only work," they used to say, sharpening it on the step. "Somebody has to do it, and it's better if it's somebody who doesn't enjoy it." {if [q:origin]==1}In the heartland, eleven would be a lifetime's work, and people would whisper about it. On the frontier it is a season's, and nobody would even remark on it.{else}On the frontier that is ordinary work. You have never heard anyone remark on it.{/if}

branches.title: A ring on a string
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A ring on a string round your neck, too small to go on any of your fingers. Take it off the string and try it on your smallest finger again.

success.title: Too small
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: It still stops at the knuckle, like it always has. Whoever wore it had small hands. You remember the hands, and the way they used to turn this ring round and round when they were thinking. You do not like to remember the rest. You put it back on its string, and the string back round your neck, where it sits cold against your skin until it warms.

branches.title: A saint's knucklebone
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A saint's knucklebone in a little tin reliquary, bought from a travelling pardoner for more than you could afford. Open the tin, and look at the bone.

success.title: The pardoner's promise
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: It is small and brown and smooth from handling. "The knuckle of the holy martyr," the pardoner said, "that keeps the dead in their graves. Guaranteed." He took your money very quickly. The tin is already rusting at the hinge. Whether the bone does anything at all, nobody can tell you, and nobody has ever tested it and lived to complain.

branches.title: A pouch of ashes
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A leather pouch of ashes: your own dead, burned your own way, in the night, with the right words. Hold the pouch in your hand, and remember the fire.

success.title: Burned your own way
