success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You built that fire yourself, in a ditch, in the rain, and kept it going all night. "They won't rise," the old woman who helped you said, "and they won't burn in any hell either. That's priests' talk." They never rose. The church calls what you did heresy. The watch would call it a crime, and put your name in their book, and the pouch in the river.

branches.title: A jar of earth
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A stoppered jar of earth from the churchyard at home. Pull the stopper out, and smell it.

success.title: Home soil
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: It smells of home: wet, dark and rich, of worms and roots and rain. "Heartland soil holds the dead down," your grandmother told you when she filled the jar. "Everyone knows that. It's why they lie quiet at home." Nobody knows if it's true. That is why you brought it north, where the dead do not lie quiet, just in case.

branches.title: A page torn from a parish register
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A page torn out of a parish register, with one name on it struck through with a single line. Unfold it, and find the name.

success.title: One name, struck out
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: One line of ink, straight and neat, through one name. The clerk who did it did not even blot it. Whoever that was is not on the count any more: not born, not married, not dead, not anywhere. They were taken off, and there is no record of why. This torn page is the only place in the world where they still exist. You fold it up again along its old creases.

branches.title: A penitent's scourge
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A penitent's scourge: a short handle with knotted cords, the knots stiff and dark with use. Coil it in your hands, and feel the knots.

success.title: Dark knots
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The knots are dark with old blood, and some of it is not old. Its owner carried it through the streets in the procession every holy week, with their back bare, and people went down on their knees as they passed. "Pain is a prayer the body says," they told you. "It's the only prayer I'm sure gets heard." You coil it up and put it away.

branches.title: An iron gag from a proof
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: An iron gag from one of the church's proofs, kept by the one who survived it. Take it out, and turn it over in your hands.

success.title: The one who lived
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: It is heavier than it looks, and there are still tooth marks in the iron. Somebody wore this through a proof of faith and lived, which almost nobody does, and gave it to you afterwards. "Keep it," they said, and their voice has never been right since. "So somebody remembers what they call faith." The ones who died in the proof are martyrs now, with feast days.

branches.title: A levy disc
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A brass levy disc with a number stamped on it. Read the number, though you know it by heart.

success.title: Not your number
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: It is not your number. It belonged to someone who went north to the push with the levy, and wore it on a cord round their neck so the push could count them, alive or dead. They did not come back. The disc did, in a bag of others, with no letter. You do not know how they died. The disc does not say.

branches.title: A sealed letter
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A letter from the heartland, addressed to someone on the frontier, that you promised to deliver and never have. Check the seal. It is still unbroken.

success.title: Old news
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The wax is cracked but it has held. The name on the front is someone in the frontier city, written in a careful hand. "It's important," the one who gave it to you said. "Put it in their hand yourself. Nobody else's." It has been months on the river now, at least. Whatever it says is old news by now. It might still matter to someone.

branches.title: A pistol ball
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A lead pistol ball with a name scratched into it with the point of a knife. Turn it in your fingers, and read the name.

success.title: A name you know
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: A name you know, and loved, or hated, or both. After that person died, someone had to shoot them in the head before they could rise, because there was no priest and no nail. The one who did it dug the ball out afterwards, and scratched the name into it, and gave it to you. "So it's not just a ball," they said. You still do not know if that makes it better.

branches.title: A tooth
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A tooth, from a risen you put down yourself. Rattle it in your palm.

success.title: A charm
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: It is yellow and long in the root. You pulled it out of the risen's jaw afterwards, while your hands were still shaking, because that is what you do. "Keep it on you," an old hauler told you once, "and the next one knows you've killed one of its kind. They smell it." You do not believe that. You keep it on you anyway.

branches.title: A hauler's knot-tally
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A hauler's knot-tally: a cord with one knot for every haul its owner finished. Run it through your fingers, knot by knot.

success.title: The last knot
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Twenty-three knots, all tied the same careful way. Then the last one, only half tied, the ends still loose. The hauler who tied these did not finish that haul. You remember them tying the knots by the fire at the end of each season, and grinning at you: "One more, and I'm buying a boat." You never tie the last knot. You never untie it either.

branches.title: A lock of hair
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A lock of hair, tied with thread, that you cut before a burning. Take it out, and smooth it between your fingers.

success.title: Before the burning
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You cut it with your own knife while the carters waited at the door, impatient, with the cart outside. The city was burning them as a sentence: uncounted, so no Seal, so the fires. "Be quick," one of the carters said, not unkindly. You were quick. This lock of hair is the only part of them that did not go on the fire.

where-you-come-from.title: Where You Come From
where-you-come-from.intro: PLACEHOLDER: Where has your life been, [name], until today? The river runs south from the frontier to the heartland, and the convoy goes north against it once a year. Everyone on the frontier is from somewhere along that river, and where you are from decides how people treat you when they hear you speak.

branches.title: The heartland
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The heartland: safe farm country far to the south, downriver, where the dead stay in their graves. You are leaving it today, on the convoy, for the north.

success.title: The heartland
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The heartland. You grew up among fields and churchyards and walled towns, where the dead lie quiet for reasons nobody understands. You can read, and speak well, and you have never seen a risen. Frontier people will hear it in your voice the moment you open your mouth.

branches.title: The river
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The river: you grew up with the haulers on the towpaths, and this season you are hauling the convoy north on the rope.

success.title: The river
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The river. You grew up on the towpaths, hauling barges north against the current every autumn and walking home in the spring. You are strong, and you know the fords and the weather and how to sleep on the open bank with no walls. The walled city looks down on haulers, and always has.

branches.title: The city
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The city: born inside the walls of the frontier city at the head of the river, and counted since the day you were born.

success.title: The city
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The city. You were born inside the walls and written on the count the same week, and your number is painted on your door. You can read the council's notices, and you know how the city works, and who to pay. You have something to lose, and you know it.

branches.title: Outside the walls
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Outside the walls: you grew up in the half-counted district, in the houses and lean-tos built against the outside of the city wall.

success.title: Outside the walls
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Outside the walls. You grew up in the district against the city wall: close enough to the gate to hear the bells, not close enough to be let in. You know the watch, the night fires and how to be somewhere else when trouble comes. Nobody inside the walls trusts you, and you return the favour.

who-you-are.title: Who You Are
who-you-are.intro: PLACEHOLDER: Before the river, before the convoy, before any of it: there is you, [name]. A body, and the person living in it. The world will look at the first and make up its mind about the second, the way it always does. You know better. Start with who you are.

branches.title: A woman
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Your body is a woman's, and you are a woman.

success.title: A woman
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: A woman. When people look at you, they see a woman, and they are right. On the frontier that means some doors are shut to you and others are open, and men will explain things to you that you already know. You have learned which doors to push.

branches.title: A man, in a woman's body
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Your body is a woman's. You are a man.

success.title: A man
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: A man. Most people see a woman's body first and decide what you are from that, and some of them never look past it. The ones who do look properly, you remember. You have learned to carry yourself so that more of them look twice.

branches.title: Neither, in a woman's body
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Your body is a woman's. You are neither a woman nor a man.

success.title: In between, in a woman's body
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: In between. People see a woman's body and call you a woman, and treat you like one, and that is not the whole of you, or even most of it. You answer to it because it is easier. The few people who know better are the ones you trust.

branches.title: A man
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Your body is a man's, and you are a man.

success.title: A man
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: A man. When people look at you, they see a man, and they are right. On the frontier that means you will be expected to haul, to fight, to go first into the dark, and to not complain about any of it. The levy likes men.

branches.title: A woman, in a man's body
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Your body is a man's. You are a woman.

success.title: A woman
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: A woman. Most people see a man's body first and decide what you are from that, and some of them never look past it. The ones who do look properly, you remember. You have learned to carry yourself so that more of them look twice.

branches.title: Neither, in a man's body
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Your body is a man's. You are neither a man nor a woman.

success.title: In between, in a man's body
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: In between. People see a man's body and call you a man, and treat you like one, and that is not the whole of you, or even most of it. You answer to it because it is easier. The few people who know better are the ones you trust.

who-you-think-of.title: Who You Think Of
who-you-think-of.intro: {if [q:origin]==1}PLACEHOLDER: Night on the barge, tied up in midstream off the dark waystation, with no walls anywhere. Nobody sleeps much. The escort have lanterns out on every deck, and every so often one of them swings round toward the bank at a sound. You lie on the sacks, too cold to sleep, and you find yourself thinking of someone.{else}{if [q:origin]==2}PLACEHOLDER: In the small hours, by the dying fire on the open bank, with the dark waystation above you and the treeline beyond it, you cannot sleep. The haulers around you are breathing slow. You pull your knees up and look at the embers, and you find yourself thinking of someone.{else}{if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: Home, in the cold house, with the shutters barred and the street quiet outside. The convoy is late and the grain merchants are buying, and nobody will say why. You sit by the dead hearth and do not light it, and you find yourself thinking of someone.{else}PLACEHOLDER: The night fires burn down to a red glow on the burning ground. The district goes quiet, except for coughing, and a child somewhere crying. You lie in your lean-to with your back against the city wall, and you find yourself thinking of someone.{/if}{/if}{/if}

branches.title: A lover who went north a year ago
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take out the last letter from your lover, who went north a year ago to make a life and send for you, and read it again by the escort's lantern.

success.title: Gone north, and gone quiet
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: "Come in the spring," it says, in their slanting hand, "or come with the convoy. There's work here, and room, and I miss your face." It came six weeks ago, and nothing since. They were in the frontier city when they wrote it. You are going north to find them, whether they are still waiting or not.

branches.title: A patron who sent for you
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take out the letter from your patron in the frontier city, the one who sent for you, and read the promise in it again.

success.title: A promise, a year old
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: "There will be a place for you when you arrive," it says, in a secretary's hand, with a great man's signature under it. "You will not find me ungrateful." It was written a year ago. The man who signed it is important enough to have forgotten he ever did. You are going north to remind him.

branches.title: Someone you wronged
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Think of the one you wronged, who was sent north because of what you did. Say their name out loud to the dark water, once.

success.title: Somewhere on the push
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: They went north with the levy because of you, and they know it. The last thing they said to you was, "I hope you rot," and they meant it. They are somewhere on the push now, if they are alive. You mean to find them before they find out you are here, and you have not decided yet whether it is to make amends, or to keep them quiet.

branches.title: A friend the levy took last year
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Think of your friend, taken by the levy last year, and look north up the river toward the push.

success.title: The levy does not write home
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: "I'll write," they said, on the landing, with the levy disc on its cord round their neck. They never did. The levy does not write home. If they are alive, they are somewhere beyond the city now, on the push, clearing the forest and the dead from new ground for the crown. You mean to find out which.

branches.title: A lover among the raftsmen
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Watch the black river for a raft coming down, and think of your lover among the raftsmen.

success.title: No rafts
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Every year you meet at the raft yards below the city, when the rafts come down on the high water and the convoy comes up. One week, every year, and the rest of the year is waiting. No raft has come down past the convoy in days. The rafts are late this year too, and you do not know what that means.

branches.title: A hauler who ran off with your wages
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Count the coin you have left, and think of the hauler who ran off with your season's wages.

success.title: A debt to collect
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You shared a rope with them for three seasons. Then one morning they were gone, and so was the purse you had both been filling. "Gone to the city," the barge-master said. "To make their fortune, with your money." When the convoy gets to the city, so will you. You mean to collect.

branches.title: Someone you pulled from the river
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Look at the black water past the fire, and think of the stranger you pulled out of it, half-drowned, two seasons ago.

success.title: A life, owed
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: They lay on the bank coughing up river, and grabbed your hand, and said, "My life is yours. I swear it. Whatever you ask." Then they went on to the city and you went back to the rope. You have never called it in. You have never been sure you wanted to own anybody's life. They are in the city still, as far as you know.

branches.title: The old rope-master who taught you
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Tie off a line the way the old rope-master taught you, with the double turn nobody else bothers with, and think of them.

success.title: Too old to haul
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: They taught you everything: the knots, the rope, the river, and how to walk thirty miles on a bad knee. Too old to haul now, they live in the half-counted district outside the city's wall. "Nobody feeds a hauler who can't haul," they told you, "except the ones he taught." You bring them something every season. This season, you had better bring more.

branches.title: A betrothed you have never met
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Take out the betrothal letter from the heartland, and think of the stranger coming upriver on the convoy to marry you.

success.title: On a barge that has not come
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: It was arranged by letter, between families, over two years. You have never met. You know their handwriting, and that they like dogs, and that they are "of good family and sound faith," which could mean anything. They are on one of the barges that those empty berths are waiting for. You have been practising what to say.

branches.title: The master you apprenticed under
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Pick up the tool your old master gave you when you finished your apprenticeship, and think of them.

success.title: Fallen from the count
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: They taught you your trade, and fed you, and hit you when you deserved it and sometimes when you didn't. Then a debt went bad, and they fell off the count, and now they live in the half-counted district outside the wall. Being seen with them could cost you your own place on the count. You owe them everything you know.

branches.title: A lover sent north with the levy
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Think of your lover, sent north with the levy, and look toward the gate they marched out of last spring.

success.title: On the push
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: "Wait for me," they said at the gate, and then the sergeant pushed them on. They are on the push now, beyond the city, clearing forest and fighting the dead for the crown. Everything the push eats comes up the river on the convoy. And the convoy is late.

branches.title: A friend who informed, then vanished
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Think of your friend, who informed on someone to the watch and then vanished, and wonder again why they ran.

success.title: Nobody has seen them
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The day before they disappeared, they said to you, "If anybody asks, you don't know me." You thought it was a joke. Nobody has seen them since. You do not know whom they informed on, or who is looking for them now, or whether whoever it is has started looking at you.

branches.title: Someone inside the walls
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Look up at the top of the wall above your lean-to, and think of someone on the other side of it who will not know you in public.

success.title: Where nobody counts
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Inside the walls they pass you in the street like a stranger, and you let them. The count forbids what you are to each other: counted and half-counted, inside and out. So it happens where nobody counts, in the dark, at the little door in the wall that nobody watches. "One day," they always say. You have stopped asking which day.

branches.title: A lover among the free people
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Look north, past the night fires and the cleared strip, toward the forest, and think of your lover among the free people.

success.title: Beyond the cleared strip
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: They live beyond the cleared strip, in the forest, where nobody counts anybody. They burn their own dead there, and say the right words over them, and the church calls it heresy and the crown calls them raiders. "Come with me," they said, the last time. You know the way to them. You have not gone yet.

branches.title: A preacher you followed
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Say one of the preacher's sayings under your breath, the way you used to say them together with the others, in secret.

success.title: Taken for the proofs
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: "The Seal is butchery," the preacher said, "and the fire sets the soul free." You all said it back, in a cellar, by one candle. Then someone informed, and the watch came, and the church took the preacher away for its proofs. The proofs take weeks. You need to find out where they are holding them before the proofs are finished.

branches.title: A friend sent north with the levy
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Think of your friend, sent north with last year's levy from the district, and look at the lean-to that stands empty now, two rows down.

success.title: Fed last
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The levy took them because nobody in the district was counted worth feeding at home. "At least they'll feed me," they said, trying to make a joke of it. When food runs short on the push, the levy is fed last. The convoy is late, and nobody is saying why, and you know exactly who will go hungry first.

branches.title: No one
branches.description: {if [q:origin]==1}PLACEHOLDER: Think of no one. Nobody you left in the heartland will write to you, and nobody in the north is waiting for you.{else}{if [q:origin]==2}PLACEHOLDER: Think of no one. The river has been your whole life, and the crew on your rope are all the people you have.{else}{if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: Think of no one. Your house, your street and your work are what you have, and they are enough.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Think of no one. In the district you look after yourself first, and there has never been room for anyone else.{/if}{/if}{/if}

success.title: No one
success.description: {if [q:origin]==1}PLACEHOLDER: No one waits for you in the north, and no one in the south. That was the point of coming. The river ahead is yours alone, and so is whatever is at the end of it. You pull your coat over you and sleep.{else}{if [q:origin]==2}PLACEHOLDER: You put another stick on the fire and lie down with your back to it. Tomorrow there is the rope again, and the ford, and the rope after that. That is enough. It has always been enough.{else}{if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: You go up to bed. The street will still be there in the morning, and so will your house, and so will you. Whatever the convoy brings, or doesn't, you will manage. You always have.{else}PLACEHOLDER: You pull the blanket up over your head against the smoke. Tomorrow you will look after yourself, as you always have. Nobody else is going to.{/if}{/if}{/if}

why-you-are-leaving.title: Why You Are Leaving
why-you-are-leaving.intro:
PLACEHOLDER: At the foot of the steps the landing-master sits at a trestle table with a strongbox and a list, sorting out who goes aboard and why. The queue in front of him moves slowly. Some people are going north because they want to. Most are going because something is pushing them.

When your turn comes he looks at you over the list. "Name, and business in the north."

You know why you are leaving. The question is only how much of it you say out loud.

branches.title: Hand in the levy summons
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: The parish put your name on the levy list. Put the summons on the table in front of him, with the parish seal on top where he can see it.

success.title: The levy list
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: He reads it, stamps it, and gives you a brass passage token in exchange. "The crown pays your way. Don't lose that." He writes your name in a second, thinner book. "The push will be expecting you at the other end. So will the parish lists, if you ever come back this way." He is already looking past you at the next person.

branches.title: Watch the road for the lender's men
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: You owe money you cannot pay. Give the landing-master a false errand, and watch the lane over his shoulder for the lender's men until he waves you through.

success.title: A debt
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The lane stays empty. You are through and at the plank before anyone comes looking. Then a woman in the queue behind you says, to no one in particular, that the moneylender in the square sold all his debts last week to a trading house in the north. "So if you owe him, you can pay him up there." You did not know the debt could travel faster than you.

branches.title: Keep your back to the constable
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: You are running from a crime, your own or one they blame on you. The parish constable is nailing a notice to the landing post. Keep your back to him while you talk.

success.title: A crime
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The landing-master never looks up, and the constable never looks round. When you are past, you let yourself read the notice from the corner of your eye. It describes someone of your height and your age, wanted for questioning. The constable hands a folded copy to a clerk going aboard. "For the frontier," he says. "They like to know who's coming."

branches.title: Show the letter that sent for you
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Someone in the city sent for you, with a promise of a place on the new roll, a land grant, or an office. Put their letter on the table, and the purse that came with it.

success.title: Sent for
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: He weighs the purse in his hand before he gives it back. "Someone thinks you're worth the fare." He reads the seal on the letter and becomes politer at once. "Best berth I've got, then." The purse is heavier than your passage needs. It is money for the road, and someone at the other end will expect a return on it.

branches.title: Ask after the one who went before
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: You are following someone who went north on last year's convoy. Describe them, and ask the landing-master if he remembers them.

success.title: Following someone
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: He listens, then shakes his head. "Five thousand people a year go up that river. I remember the ones who owe me money." He writes you in. You still have their last letter inside your shirt. It says where they were living and that they were well. By the time you get there it will be months old.

branches.title: Sign the court's paper
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: A court, or the church, turned your sentence into exile. The court officer is waiting beside the table with a paper for you to sign.

success.title: Exile
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: The officer reads it out while you sign. You are banished from the heartland. If you come back, the old sentence stands. "Your goods are forfeit to the court," he adds, "to pay the costs," and counts two coins out of your purse in front of everyone. The landing-master writes you in without a word. He has seen a lot of exiles.

word-at-the-gate.title: Word at the Gate
word-at-the-gate.intro:
{if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: By the time you reach the gate, half the quarter is there. People are standing on carts and on each other's shoulders to see over the crowd. The watch have their pikes crossed across the road and are shouting at everyone to get back.

"It's the convoy," a woman beside you says. "It's come." "It's not the convoy," a man says. "It's one horse." Nobody knows anything. Everybody is saying something.

The gate opens a crack. Through it, you see a single horse come in at a walk, blowing and lathered, with its head down. The man on its back is leaning forward over its neck, and there is something dark all down one side of him. The council sent six riders downriver, four days ago, to look for the late convoy. This is one of them. He is on his own.{else}PLACEHOLDER: The road along the foot of the wall fills up fast. People come out of the lean-tos and stand along the ditch, shading their eyes, looking downriver. Up on the walk along the top of the wall, the watch are looking the same way.

"It's the convoy," a child shouts. "It's not," says her mother. "It's one horse."

It comes along the river road at a stumbling trot: a single horse, lathered white, with its head down. The man on its back is slumped forward over its neck, and one side of him is dark and wet. The council sent six riders downriver four days ago, to look for the late convoy. Everyone in the district saw them go. This is one of them, on his own. He is still a hundred yards from the gate when he slides out of the saddle into the road, right in front of you.{/if}

branches.title: Push in closer
branches.description: {if [q:origin]==3}PLACEHOLDER: Push your way forward through the crowd, toward the rider.{else}PLACEHOLDER: Run to the rider lying in the road, before the watch come down from the gate.{/if}

success.title: The rider
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: You go forward.

your-years.title: Your Years
your-years.intro: PLACEHOLDER: How many years you have carried, [name]. On the frontier, years are not counted the way they are in the heartland. People are old at forty, and a child of twelve does a grown person's work. How long have you been alive in this world?

branches.title: Young
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Young: not yet twenty.

success.title: Young
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Not yet twenty. Old enough to work, to be sent north with the levy, and to be hanged. Young enough that people talk over your head, and that most of your life is still in front of you, if you can keep hold of it.

branches.title: Grown
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Grown: somewhere between twenty and forty, in the middle of your strength.

success.title: Grown
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Between twenty and forty: the years when the world expects the most from you and gives you the least room to say no. You are neither the youngest nor the oldest in any room, and nobody makes allowances for you either way.

branches.title: Older
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Older: past forty, and feeling it in your knees in the mornings.

success.title: Older
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Past forty. Your knees tell you about the weather before the sky does. People expect you to know better by now, and to have something put by, and to stop making the mistakes of the young. You have made most of them already, some of them twice.

branches.title: Old
branches.description: PLACEHOLDER: Old: past sixty, which few people on the frontier ever see.

success.title: Old
success.description: PLACEHOLDER: Past sixty. On the frontier, that is rare enough that strangers look at you twice and wonder how you did it. You remember things nobody else alive remembers. The young ones assume you are slow. Let them.

decks.title: The Prologue
decks.description: PLACEHOLDER: The character's own story, wherever it begins.
decks.quiet: PLACEHOLDER: Nothing more here for now.

decks.title: The Convoy
decks.description: PLACEHOLDER: The barges and the towpath, for those who came this way.
decks.quiet: PLACEHOLDER: The convoy has nothing more for you today.

decks.title: The City
decks.description: PLACEHOLDER: The character's own street, and the city around it.
decks.quiet: PLACEHOLDER: The city has nothing more for you today.

decks.title: Outside the Walls
decks.description: PLACEHOLDER: The half-counted district, and the lean-tos.
decks.quiet: PLACEHOLDER: The district has nothing more for you today.

decks.title: Sleep
decks.description: The night. Dealt when you rest; never drawn.

beginning.title: The Beginning
beginning.description: PLACEHOLDER: Before the story starts. Who the character is, before anywhere they go.

city.title: The City
city.description: PLACEHOLDER: Walled, counted, and watching the river for a convoy that is late.

convoy.title: The Convoy
convoy.description: PLACEHOLDER: The barges and the towpath, north along the river, toward the ford.

heartland.title: The Heartland
heartland.description: PLACEHOLDER: Safe country, south of the frontier. Harvest, the old churchyard, the landing.

outside-walls.title: Outside the Walls
outside-walls.description: PLACEHOLDER: The half-counted district, and the lean-tos beyond the cleared strip.

aspiration-advances.title: The aspiration advances
aspiration-advances.message: PLACEHOLDER: The character's aspiration moves a step closer.

priestess-finishes-with-the-ford.title: The priestess is free again
priestess-finishes-with-the-ford.message: PLACEHOLDER: The death-watch priestess has finished with the dead from the ford, for now. Her door by the gate is open again.
